GRAHAM (Minister of Railways and Canals) moved that the House

do to-morrow go into Committee of the Whole to consider the following proposed resolutions :
1.	Resolved, that the government of Canada may aid and assist the construction of a line of railway of the Edmonton, Yukon and Pacific Company, hereinafter called 'the company/ from a point on the company's line of railway, or on the line of railway of the Edmonton and Slave Lake Railway Company, at or near Edmonton or Strathcona, in the province of Alberta, thence, in a generally western direction, to the coal areas, situated at or near the Brazeau river and the headwaters of the McLeod river, for a distance not exceeding one hundred and fifty miles, by guaranteeing the principal and interest of the bonds, debentures, debenture stock or other securities, hereinafter called ' securities,' secured as hereinafter mentioned, of the said company, or of its successors by amalgamation as hereinafter provided, to the extent of thirteen thousand dollars per mile for the first fifty miles of the line so aided, and, for the remainder of the said line, to the amount of twenty-five thousand dollars per mile, not exceeding in all one hundred and fifty miles, the interest upon the said securities to be at the rate of three and one-half per cent per annum, payable half-yearly, the principal to bo payable in fifty years.
2.	Resolved, that the said securities so guaranteed shall be secured by a deed or deeds of trust, by way of mortgage or charge, to a trustee or trustees, approved of by the Governor in Council, and such deed or deeds of trust shall respectively grant a first mortgage or charge upon the said line of railway so aided, and the right of way, station grounds, or other real estate and interest therein, buildings and other structures and improve inents, rolling stock and equipment, plant, machinery, tools, supplies, materials, and other personal properties, present and future, acquired for the purposes of the said line so aided, and in connection with operating, repairing and maintaining it, and the tolls, incomes and revenues of the company arising and to arise from the said line, and the rights, privileges, franchises and powers of the company now or hereafter held with respect to and in connection with the said line and the operation maintenance and repair thereof.
3.	Resolved, that the deed or deeds of trust shall also create a mortgage, or charge, upon all other lines of railway and properties of the company, and upon all the property and franchises, tools, incomes and revenues connected therewith, to rank thereon next after the bonds, debentures, debenture stocks or other securities theretofore issued by the company, and next after any existing deed or deeds of trust by way of mortgage or charge securing them : provided always that, with respect to lines of railway or parts thereof now constructed and in operation, for the mileage of which no bonds, debentures, debenture stock or other securities have yet been issued, the company may issue first mortgage securities at a rate not exceeding twenty thousand dollars per mile, and may secure them by deed or deeds of trust by way of first mortgage or charge, having priority over the mortgage or charge created by the deed or deeds of trust hereinbefore mentioned.

4.	Resolved that the kind of securities to be guaranteed as aforesaid and the forms thereof, and the form and terms of the deed or deeds securing them, and the times and manner of the issue of securities and the disposition of the moneys to be raised thereon, by sale, pledge, or otherwise, pending the expenditure of such moneys for the purpose of the line of railway so aided, and the forms and manner of guarantee, shall be such as the Governor in Council approves of, and such terms, provisions and conditions may be included in such deed or deeds of trust as the Governor in Council deems expedient or necessary.
5.	Resolved, that the said guarantee shall be signed by the Minister of Finance or such officer as is. designated by the Governor in Council to sign it ; and upon being so signed the government shall become liable as guarantor for the payment of the principal and interest of the securities so guaranteed according to the tenor thereof, and the said payments shall form a charge upon the Consolidated Revenue Fund.
6.	Resolved, that the rates and tolls charged by the company upon any of its lines shall not in any case be higher than the rates or tolls fixed in the contract to be made between the government of Canada and the company.
7.	Resolved, that any moneys paid by the government of Canada under any guarantee herein provided for, shall be held to be paid in discharge of the liability of the government and not in discharge of the liability of the company under the securities so guaranteed, or under any deed of trust securing them, and the moneys so paid shall be held to be still secured by the said securities and deed of trust, and the government shall be subrogated in and to all the rights of the holders of such securities, the interest upon or the principal of which has been paid by the government, and the government shall, with respect to all moneys so paid, be in all respects in the position of security holders with respect to whose securities default has been made in payment to the extent of the moneys paid by the government.
8.	Resolved, that the guarantee of securities, as herein provided, for the said line of railway shall not be given until the Edmonton, Yukon ' and Pacific Railway Company and the Canadian Northern Railway Company have amalgamated into one company under the name of the Canadian Northern Railway Company, nor until the amalgamated company, as successors by such amalgamation, has become, as maker of the securities, liable for the payment of the principal and interest of the securities so to be guaranteed with respect to such line of railway.
9.	Resolved, that the decision of the Governor in Council as to the length of the mileage of the said line of railway so to be aided, shall, for the purpose hereof, be final. *
10.	Resolved, that the books of the company shall at all times be open for inspection for and on behalf of the government by any person named in that behalf by the Governor in Council or the Minister of Finance.
He said :	His Excellency the Governor
General having been apprised of the subject matter of this resolution commends it

to the favourable consideration of this House.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The hon. gentleman is perhaps aware from the public press that the treaty, though approved by the French Chamber of Deputies, has not been approved by the Senate. I am advised that the French Senate has adjourned and will not meet again for some weeks. We still anticipate that the treaty will be ratified, though we are not in a position to make any statement in regard to that. We are aware that the French government are making every effort to secure the French Senate's approval of the treaty, and we hope that in the end that approval will be given. In the meantime the old treaty remains in force. Until the formal approval of the new treaty by the French Chambers and the parliament of Canada takes place the matter stands precisely as before-as if nothing had been done.

I do not (think any contract has been made yet.

What I suggested was that until it is seen whether or not the French Chambers will ratify the treaty, I suppose that no steps will be taken to establish that line. I would like to ask the Minister of Railways and Canals if any arrangement has been made by which the large manufacturing establishments at Cornwall will get a greater amount of water for power than they are now getting. I understand that since the unfortunate break in the canal they have been cut down to a very small amount, w3hich puts them at a great disadvantage. I recognize that the navigation is the first point to be considered, but I understand that without any great additional expense the channel could be widened in such a way that the cotton mills and the other mills could have a larger amount of water than they are now getting. I may say that the loss of power means to one industry alone an additional expenditure of some $15,000 a month. I saw that a deputation waited on the Minister of Railways and Canals the day before yesterday in reference to this matter, and I want to know if any arrangement has been made by which the mills can get more water.

speakeroldname: Hon. GEO. P. GRAHAM (Minister of Railways and Canals).
speechtext: As my hon. friend says, the restoration of navigation is the supreme object. That is being done as quickly as possible. We cannot allow anything .to be done that is at all liable to place us at the risk of another accident of that kind. There is a large dam of a horseshoe shape. One of the difficulties found is if the current is allowed to be made fairly swift steamers coming down are liable to strike that dam, and it might be carried away and we would be in trouble again.
The currents will go away from the dam towards the mill.

Coming from the west is the difficulty. I discussed with the engineer last night the whole situation. He informed me that the curve in the canal was too sharp. I went over a rough sketch, and we decided it would be wise in the interests of navigation, apart from any consideration of the mills altogether, to widen out in one or two places so as to make the turn for vessels a little easier and ensure the safety of the cribwork as

well as improving navigation. He has also put in a crib west of the dam, so that vessels will strike the crib first and avoid the dam. It would be in the interests of navigation to widen out the channel in one or two spots, and that would also give the mills more water.

Has the hon. gentleman inquired into the accuracy of the statement made that about a year ago the department was notified of the liability of a break at this point in the Cornwall canal? It is understood that Captain Donnelly had made that statement.

The department are not able to find any such communication. The bank all along certain parts of the canal is a difficult bank to protect, and certain opinions have been expressed verbally, but I never heard any suggestion that there was danger of a break at this particular point.

St. Marys, Ont., December 13, 1901. Hon. Sydny Fisher,
Minister of Agriculture, Ottawa.
Dear Sir,-Mr. Dunbar has asked me to forward you the inclosed letter from him in reference to a very unfortunate loss of valuable stock that has come to the Messrs. Dou glas, who were Canadian exhibitors at the St. Louis fair.
I am not aware of your departmental re gulations in regard to the destruction of such diseased animals, and in regard to recouping owners for loss.

Messrs. Douglas & Son had their case In the hands of a lawyer, Mr. Dunbar, of Mitchell. He gets in touch with the sitting member of the county who <Lius writes to the minister on behalf of these gentlemen. And, after some little correspondence-and an alteration in the Act, I may say-compensation at these enormous prices is paid by the minister. I have statements before me from other veterinaries who examined these hogs, and in view of these it seems surprising that compensation should be awarded. On November 3, 1904, a letter was written to Mr. M. B. Perdue, V.S., by Dr. Rutherford in the course of which he says, 'It is very important that the diagnosis should bo placed beyond question as the animals are valuable and under the regulations it will be impossible to pay compensation. I shall not go at length into this case, but I would like to point out what the rega lations say as to payment of compensation :
1.	Hogs affected with hog cholera or swine plague, or which have been in contact with or close proximity to hogs affected with either of the said diseases should on an order signed by a duly appointed inspector of the Department of Agriculture be forthwith slaughtered and the carcasses disposed of as in such order prescribed.
5. The Minister of Agriculture is hereby authorized to order compensation to he paid Mr. BLAIN.
to the owners of such hogs at the rate set forth in subsection 2 of section 12 of the Animal Contagious Diseases Act, 1903, as amended by chapter 6 of the Statutes of 1904.
The amended statute provides as follows :
4. In all cases, the value of the animal should be determined by the minister or by seme person appointed by him, but should not exceed, in the case of grade animals, one hundred and fifty dollars for each horse, sixty dollars for each head of cattle, and fifteen dollars for each pig or sheep; and in the case of pure-bred animals, three hundred dollars for each horse, one hundred and fifty dollars for each head of cattle, and fifty dollars for each pig or sheep.
So you will see that if compensation was allowed at all under the Act, $50 is the highest price that could be paid by the minister for any bog. In this case the bon. gentleman has paid Messrs Douglas & Son $175 and Mr. Brethour as high as $180.
At this stage of the session, time is so piecious that I will not dwell upon the case. I have mentioned the fact to show how some of the money is going. In view of such payments the people will not be surprised that the public expenditure is increasing every year. The Minister of Agriculture Is something of a czar in his department; whatever he says must go; if he says the price to be paid is $180 it is paid, even though the regulations and the law say that $50 is the highest price that may be paid. I suppose the minister will answer that these gentlemen were contributing to the public good and adding to the reputation of Canada in respect of swine breeding. Well, these gentlemen are private dealers in western Ontario. The department did not ask them to exhibit their hogs at the St. Louis exhibition as a government exhibit; they sent them of their own free will. The correspondence here points out that hog cholera was to be found at the St. Louis exhibition and one of these lots of hogs was close to swine affected with that disease. Judging from the correspondence I am led to believe that the bogs contracted the disease not at Point Edward in quarantine, but in the St. Louis exhibition. The minister, when the matter was first brought to [DOT]his attention, said that 'at first blush' compensation could not be given. I do not know how many blushes it took before he felt free to pay these enormous prices. Then, if these gentlemen had a right to compensation, they did not require a lawyer to present their case to the department, nor did they have to ask the influence of the gentleman who represents the county. Why should that hon. gentleman be requested to interfere ? Taking it altogether, it seems to me there was party politics in this matter and pay, because of this these gentlemen must he paid their price. I do not know what their politics are-nor do I care; that is not tlv; question before us. But I think the farmers of this country will think that such prices

as $175 are to be regarded as pretty excessive to be paid by the government for com pensation for bogs that were sent for exhibition as a private business enterprise. I await an explanation from the Minister of Agriculture of the excessive prices that he has ordered to be paid these gentlemen contrary to his own Act.

I regret that the hon. gentleman (Mr. Blain) did not give me a little earlier notice of his intention to bring this subject forward. I merely got a slip of paper a few minutes ago that !he was going to deal with the subject
I rather apologize for the short notice.

The consequence is that I cannot answer the details of the case. I regret that, because I am sure there is a sufficient explanation to be given in regard to it. I have some memory of the case, but, not having had the opportunity to refresh my memory by reference to the files of the department, I cannot be sure of the details. The case was a very peculiar one, and that is why, when I first looked into it, I did not know whether there was any possibility of compensation or not. As a matter of fact, Air. Brethour and Douglas & Sons are well known hog breeders in the western part of Ontario. They were urged, not only by my department, but by the Department of Agriculture of the province of Ontario, to exhibit at the St. Louis exhibition. Efforts were made to get the stock breeders of Canada to do so, and assistance was given to them in taking their stock to St. Louis for the purpose of making a creditable showing of this country in the competition of live stock there. The result was that Canada did make a very creditable showing. My hon. friend said it was a matter of private business. 1 take exception to that. I think these men were public spirited citizens, and they were urged to take their stock to St. Louis.
Did the department solicit these gentlemen to exhibit their hogs at St. Louis as a public enterprise ?

Speaking from memory, I have no doubt that they did, though there may be nothing in the correspondence to that effect. At the same time, it is a well known fact that the Live Stock Commissioner of my department at that time went amongst the breeders of Canada and urged their taking part in the St. Louis exhibition, and the department went so far as to offer to pay extra prizes so as to encourage them to do so, and in order to get a creditable exhibit of Canadian live stock at that great exhibition.

The department did not pay the expenses of taking these hogs to
the St. Louis exhibition. Does he say they did ?
I am under the impression that we paid the expenses besides.
There is not a word about it in the correspondence.

AVell, I am speaking from memory. If my hon. friend had given me an opportunity of looking into the matter I would have been better supplied with the facts than I am now. But I do say emphatically that the department did make arrangements by which we added the live stock breeders of Canada in sending their stock to St. Louis ; just to what extent and in what manner 1 would have to refer to the files of the department to say. My hon. friend is looking up the files, there may be nothing about it there.

There is a letter addressed to the minister by Air. Dunbar, the lawyer having charge of this case, who says :
Had the exhibit been strictly a government exhibit, so that the government would have had charge of the transportation of the animals, I have no doubt that AIes9rs. Douglas & Sons would be compensated in full.

That is true. But it was not a government exhibit, the government had not charge of the animals ; at the same time the government did assist pecuniarily these gentlemen to send their stock to St. Louis. What my hon. friend says does not in any way militate against my statement. The fact that it does not appear in that file is easily explained. The matter of sending stock to St. Louis was managed by a special officer attached to the St. Louis exhibition staff, and had no concern whatever with the veterinary branch of my department who had to deal with the question of paying compensation for this stock. I fancy that anything concerning that would not appear on those files. I am speaking from memory, but at the same time I am pretty sure that I am correct. However, the hon. gentleman says that these gentlemen were engaged in a private enterprise. They were to the ex-tejnt that it was their stock they were handling, but I state again that they sent it to St. Louis on the request of the Department of Agriculture of the Dominion, and also the Department of Agriculture of the province of Ontario, who were desirous of seeing Canada well represented at the St. Louis exhibition. Now, so far as concerns the compensation paid, I have not the details, I have not the figures here. I take the figures my hon. friend gave, but I cannot discuss them because I have not got them before me. I can well believe that if more was paid than would have been paid under the ordinary operation of the Contagious Diseases of Animals Act, it was because of the exceptional circum-

stances and the exceptional character of the stock. This stock for which compensation was paid was the stock that practically swept the hoards at St. Louis and took the prizes at that great international exhibition.
Who received the prize money?

The men who owned the stock got the prize money, of course, who else would get it ? They sent their stock there, and did a credit to Canada which was of incalculable advantage to the whole stock industry of this country. I do not dispute the figures the hon. gentleman gave me, he need not hold them up, I daresay they are exact. All I say is that I have not been able to verify them. However I accept his statement that those figures are correct, and that the money was paid. But it must have been paid in consequence of the exceptional circumstances and the exceptional character of the stock.
I understood the hon. minister to say that the Ontario government paid part of the compensation to these gentlemen who took the hogs over to St. Louis.

I said nothing of the kind. I said that the Ontario government encouraged these men to send their stock to St. Louis for the purpose of making a creditable representation of Ontario stock, but 1 did not say that the Ontario government paid any compensation. I do not know whether they did or not, but I do not believe they did, because full compensation appears to have been paid by my department, and I know Mr. Brethour and Douglas & Son well enough to know that they would not ask any other government for compensation after getting it from this government. They are not that kind of men. My hon. friend has spoken about political influence. I believe that the hon. member for the riding of Perth wrote me a letter simply drawing attention to the fact that one of his constituents, or some people whom he knew, had suffered in this way. But there was nothing improper in that letter, nothing of a political nature. It was the kind of a letter that any member of this House ought to write in the interest of his constituents, and if he had not done so at the request of his constituents, he would have been wanting in his duty to the people whom he represents in this House. But so far as politics are concerned, I do not know the politics of Douglas & Sons. I do happen to know the politics of Mr. Brethour, a gentleman of w!hom I have the highest opinion as a man and as a breeder of hogs, and he is a well known Conservative. He has been asked to be the Conservative candidate in his constituency, in a certain election some years Mr. FISHER.
ago. Mr. Brethour was the one who took up this correspondence and dealt with it before Mr. Douglas ever came near us. It was Mr. Brethour who made the first request to the department, it was Mr. Brethour who made the representations to me. It is tr-ue that Dougal & Sons were with him, it is true they suffered with him and they got compensation with him. It was Mr. Brethour who came to see me about the matter before the hon. member for Perth ever made any representations to me at all.
Why was it necessary to place the case in the hands of a lawyer to get compensation if it was so freely given by my hon. friend's department ?

I do not know why it was necessary. It was not necessary to put the case in the hands of a lawyer. It would have been considered in exactly the same way if no lawyer had interfered with it. I do not know why Douglas & Sons put it into the hands of a lawyer, and I do not care. iMr. Brethour did not put it into the hands of a lawyer, but came personally to see me about the matter. At my first interview with Mr. Brethour I said : This is an unusual thing, and I will have to look into it carefully to see the exact circumstances of the case before I can pay you any compensation at all. I did look into the circumstances of the case, but as I said,- I am speaking from memory and cannot give all the details. Finally it was decided, that, as these gentlemen had suffered a very large pecuniary loss due to the death of their animals by hog cholera, they should be allowed compensation, that compensation was based on the report of one of our own veterinaries and I authorized and agreed to the payment. As for politics entering into it there was nothing of the kind as far as Mr. Brethour is concerned. I do not know anything about the politics of Douglas & Sons as I do not know them personally. I do not know that I had anything to do with them personally, but as Mr. Brethour is a gentleman whom I know as being one of the leading producers of high class hogs, if not the leading producer, and whom I had met over and over again at exhibitions and at live stock conventions, naturally he came personally to me to discuss this heavy loss of his and to ask for compensation. Compensation was ordered to be paid in the ordinary way of business and to suggest that there were any politics in the matter is absolutely out of the question.

1 have had the return in my possession for some time, I have gone through it thoroughly and I have drawn my own conclusions from it. The minister is usually of a very kindly disposition and I want to give him credit for

that. But, he seems to have got very wrathy over this return, and it is for that reason that I want to say a word or two. He cannot justify the payment of this compensation in that way. I would be very glad to invite the minister to visit my own district where we have many breeders of high class animals, who have as good a reputation as Mr. Brethour and these other gentlemen spoken of, and yet I can show by this return that these breeders were allowed $0 and $7 each for their high class hogs when they were ordered to be killed by Mr. Perdu. It i's simply outrageous that the compensation allowed in this case should have been paid because any gentleman who knows anything about farming never heard of a hog being worth $233.
Does the hon. gentleman know the price that Mr. Platt of Hamilton gets at public auction for his ihigh class cattle ?
I do not know anything about Mr. Platt of Hamilton.
These are high class hogs.
You cannot see a solitary thing in any of the correspondence relative to taking these animals to St. Louis.

If my hon. friend is fair he will acknowledge that the correspondence with regard to takiug these animals over to St. Louis would not appear in this return because it is in another branch of my department. The statement he is making is a direct insinuation that what I state is not correct.
Will the hon. gentleman lay that corresepondence on the table of the House ?
I can if the hon. gentleman will give me time.

Mr. Brown, your own veterinary surgeon and inspector at Point Edward, as shown by this return, distinctly states that these gentlemen are not entitled to compensation. That seems to me to be the most direct evidence that this compensation should not have been paid. As far as Mr. Brethour is concerned the taking of these hogs over to St. Louis was a personal matter with himself. He was a breeder seeking a larger market for his stock and I give him credit for having the personal enterprise to go to the St. Louis exhibition. From the evidence of Mr. Brown there is no question that the disease was contracted at St. Louis. It is because of the irregularities of this government that so much loss has been caused to the farmers of western Ontario and so much compensation has been asked for as these irregularities have permitted a large quantity of American pork to come into this country. I censure in the strongest terms possible the action of the
Department of Agriculture in authorizing any such payments as these to these gentleman, and I invite the Minister of Agriculture to come to my district at any time and discuss this question.

What authority had the minister to order the payment as compensation of such a large amount ? We had a case similar to this before the House last session, and in that case the minister refused to order compensation either large or small. The minister is controlled by statutory law the same as any one else. He may think that he is not but he is. The law says that where compensation is given the value of the animal shall be determined but that the conmpensa-tion shall not exceed, in the case of grade animals, a certain amount and, in the case of pure bred animals, $50 for each pig. It would be interesting to know what justification the minister has for the open violation of the law by which he must be controlled the same as any one else in making the compensation larger than the statute provides. Last year I drew to his attention a case in which an animal had been slaughtered because of tuberculosis and in that case there was an absolute refusal to give any compensation though the party could not afford to bear the loss. The animal had been killed in the interest of the health of the community. If these gentlemen were Induced to take their hogs to St. Louis for the purpose of representing the country I would naturally expect that they would be dealt with liberally as the circumstances would justify and the provision of the law permit. I would like to hear the minister's reason.
He has already spoken.
He has exhausted his reason.

Section 6. Under that section and by agreement entered into between the Superintendent Gen-ral of Indian Affairs and the purchasers ou or about April 24, 1900, hut not carried out by grant of the Crown until September, 1906 the Superintendent General of Indian Affairs sold to three gentlemen who certainly were not unfriendly to the government and particularly to the Superintendent General of Indian Affairs at that time, the present member for Brandon (Mr. Sifton), 29,301 acres of lands in those townships at the very moderate price of $9,017.50. That accompanies the application. The townships of Haviland and Fisher, and the most western sections of the township of Tilley.

There are some extraordinary features about that application. It is an application formal in its nature, of which the letter which I have read is not intended to form a part, and sets out the conditions on which the superintendent general is invited to sell these lands, the main features of which are the development of the district and the improvement of the conditions of the settlers in the neighbourhood. He sets out that the lumber companies that have been operating there have not been establishing any sawmills, but that on the contrary they have had the logs towed to a mill in the United States, to he there converted into lumber, iuferentially commenting very severely on that method, and suggesting that if he and his associates are granted these lands, they will adhere to the manufacturing conditions, establish a mill, and place a large number of settlers on the land. The condition suggested by the purchaser himself was communicated to him by Mr. Frank Pedley on the 22nd day of June, 1903, and in ithe same letter he is asked to pay the balance of the purchase money. He was under an obligation to plant an industry on this land which would he good for the district, good for the workman and good for the farmer, and I propose to show how anxious he was later on to remove these conditions and get the land freed from them. He says In his application that there was an American firm in there, that they were exporting logs and lie asserted that if he and his associates had the property (they would establish a sawmill and comply with the manufacturing conditions, so that the settlers as well as the Indians would have the benefit of a bardwood manufacturing industry on tliis land. Wbat was he doing in the meantime? I refer to a letter, dated September 17, 1903, which reads as follows :

Chicago, September 17, 1903.
To the hon.
Minister of Crown Lands,
Toronto, Canada.
Dear Sir,-A gentleman by the name of Wilson living in Berlin, Ontario, wishes to sell us 26,000 acres of timber lands as per the inclosed map, lands being shown inside the red lines. During the time that this purchaser was trying to get the mill clause abrogated it is shown by this letter that he was offering to sell the land to American firms and representing to them that the logs could be exported from Canada to the United States free of duty ito the Canadian government, representing that he could avoid all manufacturing conditions and that lie could avoid the very conditions upon which alone he could hope to get a patent of this land. That shows that ithe purchaser knew what the department was doing before the department had, made any ruling whatever about this mill. Before he had accepted or rejected the alternative proposition of the department as to the erection of a portable mill in lieu of a permanent mill this gentleman knew what he could do with the department, he knew (that he held some one in the department, perhaps at the top of the department, by the nose and he had confidence enough to go upon the American market and offer this tract of 20,000 acres free from all conditions, undertaking to say that there would be no export duty on logs to the Canadian government. That letter was written to the Minister of Crown Lands, Toronto, and forwarded to the Department of the Interior and, by the Department of the Interior, to the Indian Lands Department. It will be noted that the letter is dated on the 17th September. Let us see for a moment what that means. What is there included in these words, the ' kinds of timber subject to the conditions '? Here is the Department of Indian Affairs with its superintendent general, its deputy superintendent general, and all ithe officers of the department presumably watching the interests and carrying out the duties of their respective positions ; they have a contract entered into which requires the manufacture of this timber into lumber in Canada, that the purchaser shall establish a mill for that purpose of a certain capacity, that he shall employ the Indians where possible and that he shall plant settlers on the land. Notice is given to the department that the pur-

chaser is not complying with these conditions, that he is trying to abrogate them and that while the abrogation of the clause is under consideration by the department you have ithe department notified that this man is offering for sale in the United States the very same land free from all conditions which would prevent the export of logs to the United States. Would you say, Mr. Speaker, that that was a provident transaction entered into by a watchful, vigilant and honest Superintendent General of 'Indian Affairs ? I think not. I think if the Minister of Interior of that time who occupied the. position of Superintendent General of Indian Affairs had been honestly desirous of properly performing the duties of his department, if he had been desirous of maintaining the position of this government as trustee of the Indians, if he had been desirous of carefully guarding the interests of the district in which these lands were located, of the settlers and of those who were to get ithe benefits from the fulfilment of these conditions, from the establishment of that mill, he, when he got that letter, first, asking for the abrogation of the mill clause, and, secondly, followed by the letter from the Chicago man when the land was offered to him free from any conditions, would have said :	Mr. Purchaser, you
cannot have this land except upon the conditions stated in the application.
Would he not, had he desired honestly to adhere to the contract, itself, have notified the Chicago man at the same time that he told him the purchaser had not received his patent, that the patent could only issue and that the agreement was on condition that the mill should be erected and the logs cut into lumber in Canada and that the conditions of the agreement on which alone the land could be patented were such as to prohibit the export of timber from those limits in the log ? But what of the regulations themselves ? Here is an order in council dated April 9, 1901-a very significant date in connection with this transaction. The transaction was entered into in the latter part of 1900, and all this time the purchasers were being pressed to pay their money, the valuation had been made and the department was anxious to have it completed. It is shown by later correspondence that the land was offered for sale to American firms, that it was being held purely for speculative purposes, and we find on April 19, 1901, His Excelleucy in Council assenting to an order fixing manufacturing conditions on timber cut on Indian reserves and Indian lands in Ontario. These regulations are signed by His High Mightiness, Clifford Sifton, Superintendent General of Indian Affairs. I shall not read the conditions. They refer first to pine and second to spruce or other soft wood trees or timber. Whenever other wood than pine is mentioned, the regulations are careful to mention soft wood trees or timber not being 4164
pine. The regulations are careful not to mention but to except anything in the nature of hard wood, and hard wood is the very timber which was on this land and an industry for the manufacture of which it was a condition precedent to this application these purchasers should establish upon this land. The deputy was notified by Mr. Wilson that he would consent to nothing, that he would consent only to the employment of Indians at the current rate of wages if it was found they wen; suitable. He gets a reply from McLean, who evidently is desirous of fulfilling his duty as acting deputy Superintendent of Indian Affairs. The letter is dated November 27, 1903 :

Referring again to section 6 of the regula tions, my hon. friend the Minister of the Interior will see that I am right when I say that section 6 contemplates the sale being made with the concurrence of the Superin tendent General of Indian Affairs, absolutely in his discretion, upon such terms and conditions as he may see fit to impose. I was proceeding to show to the Minister of the Interior what the section contemplated as to application-this whole transaction by the Indian regulations, was to be separated entirely from sale of land by a local agent. A local agent, of course, would have no jurisdiction whatever over a transaction of this kind, it had to be made by the Superintendent General of Indian Affairs who had to proceed in the manner specified bv the regulations. There, Mr. Speaker, is the transaction in a nutshell. Let us see how it is worked out in a summary :
1.	A blanket application (Gale's), while preliminary selection made by purchaser: and valuator chosen by him and arranged with.
2.	A restricted area applied for by Wilson after inspection, and a valuator nominated by applicant and appointed by the minister.
3.	The department's proposition to sell subject to manufacturing and other condj-tions is made to and accepted by the applicant.
4.	The purchaser's nominee. is appointed by the government to value the land, and his valuation is sent to the department.
5.	Indian agent concurrently informs the department that this is a low valuation, and that the valuation of an experienced lumberman in the district, who has had intimate knowledge of these lands, is far in excess of the valuation received.
6.	Department rejects high valuation and accepts the lower one, and then reduces even the lower valuation.
7.	After lapse of three years all manufacturing conditions of sale are removed so as to permit of the timber being exported to United States in the log.
8.	Before abrogating these conditions department is made aware that the lands are being offered to purchasers in the United States
9.	Order in council of 1901 is passed, in which export of hardwood in the log is not prohibited or restricted.
10.	Purchase is allowed to drift along from 1900 to 1900, during which time all conditions of sale disappear, and the land is being offered in United States markets.
11.	Minister of Justice rules that interest amounting to $1,167.32 should be paid on the purchase money owing to delay in closing deal on recommendation of Minister of the Interior. This is remitted by order in council.
12.	Before patent issues to purchasers

they have arranged and completed a sale to United States firms of all the lands at a net profit to them of $91,813.50.
13.	Patent issues to purchasers without any conditions.
14.	Applicants and purchasers are (a) all political friends of Mr. Sifton, Minister of the Interior, Avho sold the land ; (b) one of them (A. E. Philp) his former law partner ; (e) and the others, D. A. Reesor and W. P. Wilson, active political workers and friends.
15.	Mr. Sifton, then Minister of the Interior, directs or wishes original application for the lands to be put in Mr. Gale's name at the office at Sault Ste. Marie at the time.
10.	By this transaction-*
(a)	The Indians are robbed of the true value of the land, the accrued interest thereon, and of the benefit of the manufacturing conditions, which would have provided them with labour.
(b)	The settlers in adjoining lots lose value of improvement, roads and settlement, as well as the sawmill and work in the same.
(c)	The district of Algoma loses an industry to which it was entitled, and its labouring men lose the work and its merchants the sale of material which would have resulted from its maintenance.
(d)	The close political friends of the minister gain $91,813.50 without cutting a tree or doing any work of improvement or development.

The worst his opponents can allege is that he has been remiss in not ordering an inquiry into the Interior Department and not dismissing those about him who make a vulgar display of riches acquired no one knows how, unless by official malversation on a grand scale.

Well, Sir, the right hon. gentleman made some professions as far back as 1893, and those professions were backed up by a gentleman. then a very modest young man, who came from the province of Manitoba and who addressed the Liberal convention, saying he was pleased to be there as representative of the youngest province of the Dominion, a young man himself in official life, as he stated. Now, Mr. Chairman. I am called upon to second a resolution affirming again the Liberal principle of economy. right to say that we are the exponents of economy. Our opponents do not even pretend to be economical. Their principle is to get all the money they can from the people and distribute it amongst their friends.
