He stated that it was the principle of his opponents to get all .the money they could from the peop'e and distribute it amongst their friends. The bon. gentleman has shown that he has followed that principle by getting all the money he could from the people and distributing it amongst his friends, if not himself. These were the principles which were affirmed by the right hon. gentleman. Time after time grave matters of mal-administration in the Department of Indian .Affairs have been brought to the attention of the right hon. gentleman. In each case he has defended, or excused, or, if he has not defended or excused, and if he has been silent, he has been the first to rise in his place to vote down investigation, or the punishment of the offenders or that an inquiry should be held into the transaction referred to. Wherever there was a case of corruption the right hon. gentleman has defended or excused it. Where the public has been robbed he has voted down resolutions condemning the robbery. Where the public service was degraded he has denied an investigation and if public servants have been shown to have stolen from the people he has voted down inquiry, investigation, punishment or condemnation. The right hon. gentleman has lent his moral support to transactions as scandalous as this. He has upheld Siftoniau *deals, he has voted for them, he has approved them and if he does that and if he affirms before this House and the country that he does so approve of them, that he will not lend a hand to punish the offenders or even to inquire whether the accusations and information be correct, than I say that he is standing before this country at this hour, when he is about to ask for the re endorsation of the people, as one who has not elevated public morality, as one who has not done that which he professed and promised to do. which he vowed that he would do and which he pledged himself to do in his great platform and in his great speech of 1903, which induced the people of Canada to entrust to him the reins of power. The right hon. gentleman is very fond sometimes in this House of making quotations from the sayings and speeches of the Hon. Geo. Brown. He will perhaps remember this quotation from that statesman's speech which is pertinent to the position in which he finds himself to-day :
If, sir, a public man avows certain principles, agitates those principles and seeks to
overthrow a government to establish those principles, and when he attains power, laughs at his professions and casts his principles to the winds, he is aiming a blow at public morality.
I ask the right hon. gentleman to take those words to heart in conjunction with the very serious matter which I now commend to his attention and leave with him. There is not a fact that I have stated but which is referred to in the documents in his department. I am not responsible for any of them. Every one of these facts is set forth in the documents extracted from the Department of the Interior. How many more there may be that we have not seen I do not know, but I do know that there has been knitted together a case which the right tiou. leader of the government cannot excuse and cannot justify. One by one these facts have been knitted together and they disclose a transaction which is absolutely indefensible. I have embodied in the resolution which I now propose to offer to the House these facts as they appear and which I will commend to the right hon. leader of the House. Mr. Speaker, I beg to move :
I hat all the words of tile said motion after the word ' that ' be struck out, and the following substituted in lieu' thereof:
The government as trustees for the Indians is bound to sell Indian lands or timber, or other valuables thereon, for the best price obtainable, and to the best possible advantage of the Indians.
That the sale by the government of lands in the townships of Haviland, Tilley and Fisher, in the district of Algoma, with the timber thereon, containing 29,301 acres for $9,017.50 without competition to political friends who were thus enabled to reap profits amounting to $91,813.50,on re-sale of the said lands and timber made by them, before patent issued was not a sale for the best price obtainable, nor to the best possible interest of the Indians, but constituted a grave breach of trust by the government and deserves the condemnation of this House.
I have only to say in conclusion that we have recently had a most emphatic illustration of the wantonuess of this sale in which there was no competition and no public advertisement. We had a sale by public auetiou on the 24th June of Indian timber limits which produced the magnificent sum of $871,000 which went into the Indian funds where it ought to belong in exchange for the timber. In this case, by private sale, $91,000 went into the pockets of the friends and an erstwhile partner among them of the former Superintendent General of Indian Affairs who made the sale.

speakeroldname: Hon. FRANK OLIVER (Minister of the Interior).
speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I think it is proper, in discussing the question now before the House, to call attention tc what must be very prominent in the minds of all hon. members. We have before us on the Order

Paper at the end of an eight months' session
For which the government are responsible.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Ten Bills of serious importance for the consideration of the House. We have Supplementary Estimates on the table for consideration amounting to something like $10,000,000, railway subsidies of possibly $10,000,000.

Hear, hear.
Mr. OLIVER-and we have also a proposition to guarantee certain aid to railways to the amount of something like $10,000,000. There is sufficient important business to claim the best attention of the House for the remaining period of the session, whatever it may be. To occupy the time of this deliberative body for two hours and a half in shrieking into ' Hansard ' the elements of a future campaign address is neither more nor less than an outrage upon parliamentary propriety and the patience of the House. The hon. member knows that in making such a statement at such a time he must have peculiar freedom because no person could take the time or the trouble nor would the House submit to the time or trouble necessary to contradict or disprove the absurdities he has placed before us. My hon. friend, however, has shown himself wiser than the gentleman whose parable he has taken up. whose mantle he seems to think has fallen on his shoulders, the hon. member for St. Antoine Division (Mr. Ames), the slander-monger in chief of our hon. friends opposite.
Order.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: I think that expression should be withdrawn.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I withdraw it, I was so convinced of the truth of it-

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order. The hon. gentleman knows that it must be unreservedly withdrawn.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I have withdrawn it unreservedly.
There is too much of the woolly west in that.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
The member for St. Au-toine Division (Mr. Ames), if I am not allowed to use the word slander in connection with statements he made before the House, was unwise, he was not satisfied with making them here when there was not a fair opportunity of disproving them. He was so successful in his efforts on the floor of the House that he undertook to carry them further where they could be investigated with an opportunity of determining their truth or falsity, with the result that 'he has retreated from the House to make his peregrinations in the remote parts of Canada with his limelight, his camera, and his micros-Mr. OLIVER.
cope. His usefulness in the House appears to have departed-and he has departed with it. The hon. member for Algoma (Mr. Boyce) is wiser in his generation, he is careful to delay his slander

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: The hon. member has heard a moment ago that that statement should not be used.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I withdraw the term, I shall use the expression * unfounded and untruthful allegations.' He has chosen a time when the condition of business for the session does not admit under any circumstances dealing with this question either on the floor of the House or in the committee where it should be dealt with. If the one hundredth part of the noise that my hon. friend has made to-day were warranted by the facts and if he did desire to arrive at a knowledge of the facts, he has had eight months of this session, he has had from day to day the sittings of the Public Accounts Committee before which he could have brought his charges, to have proved, if possible, everything he has alleged here. I submit with due deference that allegation is not evidence, particularly at a time when such statements-and they would be grave statements if they came from a grave source-can not be dealt with as their gravity entitles them to be dealt with. My hon. friend must take it as he gives it. Having chosen to put forward these statements at a time when they cannot be proved or disproved he must accept the opinion that they are of but little weight and could not have been proved if he had brought them forward at a time when investigation would be possible.
He dare not investigate them.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
My hon. friend is perfectly safe, there is no danger of investigation between now and the close of the session. My hon. friend has been here nearly eight months, he has been an active and energetic member of the House. The alleged facts he has placed before us are within a stone's throw of where he has lived for ten or fifteen years, but he chooses an opportunity, three days before the end of the session, to bring forward the statement he has made, and which I shall not call slanderous again.
I am somewhat at a loss to know just what my hon. friend's charge is. The allegation would seem to be that certain gentlemen lived in a place called Brandon. If that is a crime, then these certain men, Messrs. Wilson, Philp and Reesor, are residents of Brandon and must be condemned. Is it a crime that this land was sold? The land is of no use to the Indians unless it is sold, It is the price that the Indians want and not the land.
Hear, hear.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: And so the land has to be sold somehow, somewhere,to some one, at some time. Thus, if I understand the matter correctly, it has been the practice of the department for twenty or thirty years, during part of which time my hon. friend was a member of the government, to make sales of Indian lands under certain circumstances. According to that practice a certain sale was made. Is that a crime? Is that the offence charged against the Superintendent of Indian Affairs of that day or whoever was responsible? If that is the crime, then we must admit they are guilty. Is it a crime that the land was sold at 30 cents an acre ? The timber of value, that is, the pine timber upon it, had already been removed under a license which had covered this same area.

My hon. friend will pardon me. The land was sold subject to the provisions of a timber lease then in existence, and that was subsequently cancelled, so that the purchasers got the benefit of the cancellation.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
I repeat that the land was sold subject to the timber license, and the licensees had exhausted their rights, and their rights were cancelled because they had no more rights to exercise, and the purchasers of the land paid extra for the balance of the pine timber that remained upon the tract, and the valuation of the timber was $66. So that the timber of value, the pine timber, had been cleared off before the sale was made. The minerals an the land were also reserved. So that what the purchasers got was the hardwood growing upon the land and the surface rights, for which th.ey paid 30 cents an acre some eight years ago. Now, I am credibly informed that in all this vast area of New Ontario any person may at the present time go anywhere and buy any piece of land for 50 cents an acre, including the mineral rights and the timber rights except the pine timber, and that after performing certain limited settlement duties, and after a period of three years, he gets a patent for the land, including the pine timber. If it as a question of price, it seems to me that the Indians got a better price for their land that was sold eight years ago than the government of the province of Ontario is getting for the land that it is selling to-day. Under these circumstances the charge that there was something wrong in the sale at that price does not seem to be substantiated.
I am mi able to follow all the charges which my hon. friend made. There was a charge that a man lived in Brandon ; there was a charge that the laud was sold ; there was a charge that it was sold at a low price ; there was a charge that it was afterwards sold at a higher price. It had been sold at a higher price, and it had been sold before the patent from the Crown had been issued. What is the charge in that statement of fact ? When a sale is made,
if the purchaser fulfils the conditions, the conveyance has to be given, although the property may increase in value. Now, my hon. friend is of the legal profession, and I do not think he will suggest that the Indian Department, having sold lands at a certain price, and the price having been paid, the department had any right to refuse the conveyance of these lands, no matter whether the right to them had changed hands or not. If he holds that view, it is a decidedly new doctrine to me, and in administering the Indian lands and the Dominion lands, I shall have to take new advice in order to be able to conform to the rule my hon. friend has laid down.
But a charge is that the land was sold at a higher price than it was purchased for. Now, I do not suppose that anybody buys anything as a commercial transaction without expecting to sell it at a higher price. That is what he buys it for ; and does my hon. friend suggest that a sale having been made, if the value of the property increases, the sale must be cancelled ? My hon. friend is not surely so absurd as to hold sueh an argument when it is stated in plain words. And yet, if there is anything in his charge, that is the position which he insists that the Department of Indian Affairs shall take. Well, let us try this question out by a parallel case. There is a member of this House who sits on the opposite side, a man of high repute, personal and financial, a man whose personal honour or whose business honour I think nobody in the House will question ; I speak of the hon. member for West Toronto (Mr. Osier). This hon. gentleman was a member of a company which had the ownership of certain lands which had been granted to the Regina, Qu'Appelle and Long Lake Railway Company. So far as the matter has come to my knowledge, this hon. gentleman was the chief agent of his associates both in acquiring these lands and in disposing of them. At a certain time, I think in the year 1902, this company-I believe, acting through the agency of the same hon. gentleman-disposed of a quarter of a million of acres of the lands at I think $1.63 an acre. To-day that land is worth $5 or $10 or $15 or possibly some of it $20 an acre. Does my hon. friend suggest that the sale that was made in good faith at the highest going price and through the agency of the hon. member for West Toronto at that time, was a dishonest sale and should be cancelled because that land is worth more today than it was then ? He would not suggest such a thing; he would say that anybody who would suggest it was not speaking with due responsibility.
And yet he stands up here and for two hours and a half he has shrieked into ' Hansard ' denunciations of a certain transaction because the value of the land went up and was sold at a higher figure in a subsequent year. I submit that the position he takes is an absurd one. To say that

because property has been sold at a certain figure at a eertain time and afterwards sold at a much higher figure, the transaction Is not honest, is to draw a conclusion utterly unwarranted. The hon. gentleman drew a comparison between the sale of land in these townships at Batchawana Bay and the sale which recently took place of the timber in the Dokis reserve. He pointed out that, in the first instance, the minister sold the land at thirty cents, and that, in the second instance, a comparatively small area of Indian lands was sold at $871,000. Sir, the comparison is far worse than that. In the case of the $871,000 sale, there was not a foot of land transferred at all. All that was sold was the right to cut the timber for ten years. It is quite possible that the tract to which the hon. gentleman alludes in the first place might have carried timber, but that timber had been cleared away, and to make a comparison between bare land, or more probably rock, and the timber on the Dokis reserve shows the absurdity of my hon. friend's argument from the beginning to the end, and it bears out the view that he would never have made the statement he did. had there been an opportunity to investigate the matter to a conclusion. I do not know that any more need be said. The transaction wa= in the ordinary line of business. It was just the same as those which had taken place in the department during the past twenty or twenty-five years. It differed from them in no particular except in this that some of these people lived at Brandon and that some of them wrote letters and some of them did not. My hon. friend (Mr. Boyce) has followed the example set him by the hon. member for St. Antoine division (Mr. Ames) and has imported into his statement of the case insinuations and suggestions entirely unworthy of being put before a deliberative body. The Indian lands are unquestionably a sacred trust. It is the duty of the government to administer them with the view of obtaining for the Indians their utmost value. These lands are looked upon by the public as a sacred trust, and the hon. gentleman is seeking to take advantage of that sentiment in making this most unfair attack especially at this period of the session. If he could prove that there was anything wrong done, he would have made a point, but he was careful to bring his accusation at a time when there could not be produced any proof.
Can the' minister give any good reason why the land was not put up at public auction ?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: This land was offered for sale in accordance with the practice of the department which had prevailed for twenty-five or thirty years or more. What was good enough iu preceding years was still considered good enough when this sale was made. And because in the process of time.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: conditions change and it becomes necessary to adopt new methods, that is no proof that the former administration was improper or dishonest. But my hon. friend jumped to the conclusion that because there has been a change of administration due to the changed conditions, there must have been something wrong with the previous administration. Nothing could be more unfair.

A few words in reply to the extraordinary defence of the Minister of the Interior. What is the charge ? The charge made by my hon. friend from Algoma (Mr. Boyce) is that the Department of the Interior, against the advice of the Deputy Superintendent General of Indian Affairs, sold property belonging to the Indians, held by us in trust, for a sum altogether inadequate to its value. The hon. gentleman has tried to defend this by citing the policy of the government in the past. Well, if there is one sacred trust which the people of this country should fulfil to the utmost letter, it is that of the Indians. If there is one thing this or any government should be most careful to see to, It is that our wards, the Indians, should receive the highest value for the small moiety of property left to them in this country. There can be no doubt as to the accuracy of the statement made by my hon. friend from Algoma. There can be no doubt that certain parties, clearly connected with the ex-Minister of the Interior (Mr. Sifton) got possession of these lands, belonging to the Indians, for a ridiculously low price, and t3he minister tries to justify this by saying that his predecessor, the ex-minister, (Mr. Sifton) only followed the precedent set him by previous administrations.
The justification pleaded by the minister is that he was following the usual course in the disposition of these Indian lands. I deny that. I give a most distinct and emphatic denial to the statement that it was the policy of the last government to dispose of these lands contrary to the very advice of the deputy superintendent general off Indian Affairs-who, in this case, it appears, declared in his report that the price for these lands was totally inadequate but was overridden by the Minister of the Interior of that day. And in this way these lands were disposed of, these lands which were held as a sacred trust by the government. I say it is a disgrace to the officers of the government and to the Minister of the Interior that such a thing should happen. Where is the authority for the Minister of the Interior to say that this was the mode by which these lands were disposed of in the past ? The policy of the late government was to ask for tenders for these lands. Nothing was more sacred in the eyes of that government than the trust they exercised in these Indian lands, and they did

all in tlieir power to see to it that the Indians got the very last farthing for all the lands that were disposed of. And not only were they careful to act according to the opinion of the chief officers administering the department, but they insisted that the Indians themselves should be a party to the surrender. I da not see anything of that kind here ; certainly it was not stated by my hon. friend (Mr. Boyce) nor was it shown by any of the documents he read that the consent of the Indians had been obtained for the sale of this property. But the bald fact stands out that parties closely connected with the Minister of the Interior of that day got control of these Indian lands, and, even before they had got the conveyance of them, they had turned them over at a profit of $90,000. And this government is trustee for these poor creatures who are not able to look after themselves, who at one time owned all the land of this country of which now but a pittance remains to them. And this is the way the Minister of the Interior of this government exercised the sacred trust reposed in him 

defrauding these poor people of whom we are the trustees of the sum of $90,000. I say it is simply a disgrace to the management of the department that anything of the kind should occur. I say that my hon. friend from West Algoma (Mr. Boyce) did right to draw the attention of the House to the vulgar ostentation of wealth of these parties from one end of the country to the other, wealth obtained by means such ns this. The people of Canada will soon have an opportunity to express their opinion of such transactions, and I hope and believe that the standard of morals among our peo pie is such that the electors will punish such crimes as these, committed by those who have thus unworthily exercised the power of government.

I desire to say Just a few words in response to the peculiar observations of the Minister of the Interior (Mr. Oliver). That hon. gentleman saw fit to apply some strong language to my hon. friend from St. Antoine, Montreal (Mr. Ames). There was good reason for his doing so. For if the minister has had certain workings of his department, which he would have preferred to conceal, exposed before this House and this country-

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I would like to know if my hon. friend is in order in saying that I desired to conceal the workings of my department ?

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: I think that that language is not in order.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I wish to say distinctly that I do not wish to conceal any part of the working of my department that is rightly the property of the public.

So far as you find my remark to be out of order, Mr. Speaker, I withdraw it. But I desire to say that it is this same hon. gentleman (Mr. Oliver) who stood up in his place here and declared that he would not bring down certain original documents which in the end he was forced to bring down. He stood in his place here and read a memorandum from his deputy, reading it as his own, which stated that these original documents should not be placed before parliament. Relying on a majority at his back in this House

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I desire to correct the hon. gentleman's statement as to that memorandum, I did not read it as my own statement, but as the advice received from my deputy. And, if I remember well, it did not say that these documents would not be brought down-very far from it.

The hon. gentleman (Mr. Oliver) declared that they should not be brought down until a special vote had been passed for that purpose in this House ; he declared that he proposed to abide by that memorandum and by the advice so received. But the hon. gentleman did not abide by that advice, because, in the end, the original documents were produced and laid on the table of this House without any special,vote of the House being demanded.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I desire to correct the hon. gentleman
I want to be correct.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I am sure of it. I objected, and stated to the House my objection, to bringing down private documents to this House, which documents, on motions calling for them being carried, and on the documents being brought down in response to those motions, became part of the records of the House and were removed from being part of the records of the department. And I instanced the case of what had occurred during the session before, when, in response to a motion by the hon. member for North Toronto (Mr. Foster), certain original documents had been brought down which became part of the records of the House and ceased to be part of the records of the department though they were needed in carrying on the business of the department. And the motions of hon. gentlemen opposite requiring the production of original documents were amended so that these documents did not become part of the records of the House but were laid upon the table for inspection and returned to the department.

The hon. gentleman (Mr. Oliver) laid great stress upon the circumstance that certain documents

had not been returned. But he knew, and every one knew, that all he had to do was to stand on his feet for thirty seconds and move for an order to return these documents to the department,

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Precisely.
BORDEN-but the hon. gentleman did not think it worth while to do so.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I did not think it my duty. The House had seen fit to make these documents part of its records. The House controls its own actions ; and, if it saw fit to do this, certainly it was not for me to take control when control had been taken from me by the House.

I suppose the hon. gentleman is not so absolutely ignorant of the rules of this House as not to know that documents can be brought down only on motion by a member of the House. If the hon. gentleman (Mr. Oliver), as custodian of these papers, requires them back, it is his duty to move to that effect.
But this is only an incident. I was referring to the fact that the hon. gentleman had good reason, even in the absence of the hon. member for St. Antoine, to use strong expressions with regard to the course which that hon. gentleman has taken In this House. And the hon. minister (Mr. Oliver) has not heard the last'of it. For, if I am not mistaken, he will hear something from that hon. gentleman in the west; and if he desires to meet my hon. friend from St. Antoine on any platform in the west, a proper amount of time will be given him to make his explanation of the administration of his department. The hon. minister referred to the postponement of this motion, but he did not see fit to say that it had been postponed at his own instance. On at least three different occasions to my knowledge, the matter has been postponed either by the action of the government, or at its request. His allusion to the circumstance that this matter has not been brought up

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I am not aware-
BORDEN-was unworthy of the hon. gentleman and one in which, it seems to me, he ought not to have indulged.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I am not aware of having been the cause of the postponement of this motion, and I would like to know when the motion was first proposed.

The day before yesterday there was an arrangement made for it, that was departed from, and another arrangement was made yesterday and that was again, at the suggestion of the government, altered and a previous arrangement to that, when it was said the hon. gentlc-Mr. R. L. BORDEN
man could not be present on account of a cabinet meeting, was the third to which I have reference. I do not know how many others there were. Under the circumstances, it did not seem to be a happy taunt from the hon. gentleman to speak of postponements. Why should it be postponed ? There is no reason for it. My hon. friend, at the earliest opportunity, was ready to bring it on as soon as he had prepared the case and was able to speak upon it; and when he was ready to bring it on, there were the delays to which I have alluded'. The minister refers to the lack of evidence. The evidence relied on by my hon. friend from Algoma is to be found in the records of the hon. gentleman's own department, brought down and laid upon the table of the House. What better evidence does he want than that?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Such part of the record as my hon. friend chooses to pick out and present,
Does the hon. gentleman say t-liat there is any other portion of the record which qualifies that which has been alluded to by my hon. friend from Algoma ?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: The best way to answer that is to bring it before a committee of the House.

We do not usuallv bring these records before a committee of the House unless there is some fact to be investigated, and inasmuch as the facts were plain and open upon this record, and inasmuch as that portion of the record mentioned by my hon. friend from Algoma is not qualified, so far as I understand, by any other portion of the record, the observation of the Minister of Interior is absolutely beside the mark, and shows his utter incapacity to make any defence whatever to the statements of my hon. friend.
The minister says the statements are grave. He is right, and there has been no answer, except the complaint of lack of time. The minister has had notice of this motion four or five days.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I never had any notice of this particular motion. I had notice that my hon. friend proposed to bring up a motion in regard to Indian lands, but I had no notice that they were the Indian lands he has alluded to.
I accept any correction of that kind.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: That is not what I was objecting to at all. I objected to his bringing this question forward at a time when the press of the business of the session is such that it cannot be attended to fully, either on the floor of the House or in a committee of the House.

BORDEiN. There is no necessity for any committee of the House, there is a necessity for investigating the records of the department which have been laid upon the table. If he has any complaint that all the facts have not been brought out, 1 will undertake to stay here an additional day, and to give him all the time from the present until next Monday, or next Tuesday, or next Wednesday, to go thoroughly through these records and show whether any of the facts stated by my hon. friend from Algoma can be controverted by the records, or in any other way, by the Minister of the Interior.
What is the gravamen of the charge of my hon. friend from Algoma? I accept the comparison of the Minister of the Interior to the ease of a private trustee. What would be thought of a private trustee, and where would he find himself, if, taking the trust property, he sold it upon the statement of a valuator selected by the purchasers, sold it under certain conditions, every one of which was afterwards abrogated, and finally handed it over for a sum of $9,000, although, before the deed was given by the trustee, the purchasers sold it to another person for $101,000? Where would any private trustee find himself under these conditions? In the first place, at the very earliest opportunity, any court of the land would hold this action up to the severest condemnation and would order immediate restitution, with interest. That would be the first proceeding. The next proceeding probably would be, if certain circumstances might fairly be taken into account, that such a trustee would probably be called upon to answer in the criminal courts upon a charge of malfeasance in his office of trustee. Why, the circumstances are almost unbelievable. If any hon. gentleman in this House had arisen and made the statement, without being able to base it upon the records of the Department of the Interior that this particular series of transactions had taken place in that department one would have said that the man was drawing upon bis imagination. And yet every line and every word he mentioned can be substantiated, and has been substantiated by my hon. friend from- Algoma, by a direct reference to the records of the Department of the Interior. There is small wonder that the Minister of the Interior takes up his half hour in making complaints as to the period at which this matter was brought to the attention of the House, and endeavouring to cast slurs and aspersions upon an hon. member wTho is not here to defend himself, and who needs no defence against any attacks that can be made upon him by the Minister of the Interior.
The Hon. gentleman had the temerity to refer to private transactions, and amongst others, to the transactions of my hon. friend from West Toronto (Mr. Osier) in connection with the sale of certain
lands which were afterwards acquired by the gentleman who had formed themselves into that wonderful corporation known as the Saskatchewan Valley Land Company. If I am not mistaken, when those lands were sold-I have for this the word of the member for West Toronto, as well as the records of the department, itself-when these lands were sold it was not known that the area within which they might be selected had been enormously increased by an order in council of this government, and that added very materially to the value of these lands. I do not doubt if the member from West Toronto had known at the time, as he has assured me he did not know, that that area had been so extended, the price he would have asked for those lands would have been very much greater. Further than that, what is the idea of the hon. gentleman in comparing a sale of agricultural lands in the west of Canada to the sale of these lands? He knows that the value of those lands, sold, as he says, by a company in which my hon. friend from West Toronto is interested, has been since Increased by settlement, and the development of that country by the influx of settlers. No such conditions prevailed in the district we are now discussing, so far as I am aware, at all events, they did not prevail up to the time of the resale by the purchasers. Will the Minister of the Interior tell me this? What was it that increased! the value of those lands from $9,000, the price received by these fortunate grantees from certain gentlemen from the United States, what was it that occurred to increase the value? Can any one doubt that if these lands had been put up at public auction, and if these gentlemen had had an opportunity to bid for them, the results would have been very different?
Another instance that is most startling in connection with the matter, is this : There was more than one report made to the government as to the value of these lands. There was a report made bv Mr. McAuley, the gentleman nominated by the very men who were purchasing from the government. That is said to have been a sworn valuation. There was another report brought to the attention of the head of the department by a man who had means of knowledge as to the value of the property. We do not know what that man's estimate was; it does not appear as far as I am aware, but it does appear in the records of the department and by the report of the deputy head of the department that the report of that independent man placed the value of this land very much above the amount stated in the report of the valuator selected by the purchaser. Imagine a private trustee acting with respect to a property which was not his own, acting under a trust, having before him two reports, one a report made by persons to whom the

land was to be sold and the other the report of an independent person,imagine him having it brought definitely and distinctly to his attention that the report of the independent person was very much larger in its estimate of the value than the report of the man who had been selected by the purchaser, imagine that trustee, in face of these circumstances, putting aside all further inquiry or investigation into the value of this land, disregarding the report of the independent valuator and taking the $9,000 report of the man who had been selected by the purchaser-imagine that in the case of a private trustee and come to a conclusion, if you please, as to what would be the result of an investigation by the courts into the conduct of any trustee such as that which has been described. The circumstances in the case being as they are I am bound to say that in my estimation, after listening with the utmost possible attention to the speech of my hon. friend the Minister of the Interior, I have heard not a single word uttered by him in defence or justification of the case which has been made out so clearly.

Mr. Speaker, I did not intend to say anything on this subject had it not been for some outside remarks that the hon. leader of the opposition (Mr. R. L. Borden) has brought in and to which I wish to refer for a moment. The leader of the opposition has said that the hon. member for West Toronto (Mr. Osier) made the statement that he was not aware, that, when the company of which he was the principal member sold some railway lands to the Saskatchewan Valley Land Company, this government, by order in council, largely increased the area of the lands and therefore made them more valuable.

I did not say that it was when the sale was made, but I said that when the hon. member for West Toronto negotiated that sale, as the Minister of the Interior has told us, he was absolutely in ignorance of the fact that the area had been extended.	.
That statement of the hon. member for West Toronto is an absolutely false statement in every shape, form and manner.
Shame; order.
I have made the same statement in the House before and the statement I make is absolutely true.
Order.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext:
I cannot very well rule on that point. A statement is made by one hon. member as to what another hon. gentleman has said and the hon. member for East Assiniboia (Mr. Turriff) states, apparently from personal knowledge, that the Mr. R. L. BORDEN
statement is untrue or false. I cannot very well rule that that is out of order.

I will say it is absolutely untrue if that will suit hon. gentlemen any better. I will say further that before the hon. member for West Toronto made the sale to the Saskatchewan Valley Land Company the Minister of the Interior of that day, on two different occasions a year apart wrote to the solicitor of the hon. member for West Toronto, the man who was handling the case that they had against the government, asking the government to give them cash in lieu of land, sending him a map and stating that there had been set apart 10,000,000 acres of land in addition to what they already had had set apart in 1887.
May I ask the hon. gentleman who the solicitor is to ijvhom he refers ?

I refer to Mr. Creelman who is at the present time the solicitor of the Canadian Pacific Railway Company, who, at that time, was solicitor for Osier, Hammond and Nanton, and who had brought action against the government to force the government to pay them cash in lieu of land on the ground that the land was absolutely unfit for settlement. In order to give them a better opportunity of locating their land, the government in 1900 and 1901, set apart four different blocks in addition to what had already been set apart, out of which they might select the 800,000 acres which were coming to them.
Who had brought action?
The Regina, Long Lake and Saskatchewan Railway Company.

I have not the records before me, but I have investigated the question very carefully. I have looked over every scrap of paper I could find in two very large returns. I looked up the case after it had been stated in the House that notice had been given, and I can find no such notice had been given, and I can find no notice given to any solicitor which would give the information which the hon. gentleman has stated. I examined the returns with great care because that statement had been made and I could find no notice such as the hon. gentleman has spoken of.

If the hon. gentleman will get a copy of the bill of rights that was presented by Osier, Hammond and Nanton on behalf of the railway he will find copies of these letters of the Minister of the Interior to their own solicitor and copies of their letters from their own solicitor back to the Minister of the Interior giving the reasons why they would not take the land in these four new blocks, and saying that they had sent their inspectors over that

land. Not only did the hon. member for West Toronto know that the land had been set apart, but they sent their inspectors over the land, their inspectors examined most of this new area of 10,000,000 acres and they reported back to the government that in the additional area they were not able to find enough land which would come up to the requirements of their contract, that is to say, which was fairly fit for settlement. The Minister of the Interior notified them that if they could not find enough laud within these four blocks and within the original blocks set apart by order in council they could then go outside of these blocks into any land which had not been selected by other railway companies and take what they could get.
What, has this to do with robbing the Indians?

It was the hon. leader of the opposition who brought this matter up. I am only replying to a statement made by your hon. leader to show that he has been misled by the hon. member for West Toronto and I am just putting the facts of the case before the House. It has nothing to do with the Indians, it has nothing to do with the matter that is under discussion, cut it was not I who brought it up; it was the hon. leader of the opposition.
My hon. friend does not desire to mislead the House, I am sure.
No.
I did not introduce it; the Minister of the Interior introduced it.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: I think it would be wise not to pursue this subject any further but to confine the discussion to the subject before the chair.

I will close in one minute. I want to say in conclusion the t the statement that has been made in this House before and which the hon. leader of the opposition has made now, on the authority of the hon. member for West Toronto, is absolutely without foundation, that there is not a word of truth in it, that when Osier, Hammond and Nanton sold the land to the Saskatchewan Valley Land Company there was an increase in the area and that if the hon. leader of the opposition wishes to go into the matter further all he needs to do is to get the bill of rights presented by Osier, Hammond and Nanton or send over to the Department of the Interior and get copies of the correspondence with respect to the matter.

I assume that ns this matter of the sale of land by the trustees of the Regina, Long Lake & Saskatchewan Railway Company has been brought under review you will, Mr. Speaker, make 417
no objection to hearing the statement which I propose to offer with reference to it?

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: I think it is not relevant to the matter under discussion. It was brought in by way of illustration, as I understand, in the first place, by the Minister of the Interior and was used in the same way by the hon. leader of the opposition. I think the discussion of it is not relevant.

As the statement was made by the Minister of the Interior in reference to my hon. friend from West Toronto (Mr. Osier), which I regard as a very unfair statement, I thought that I, would be entitled to a small modicum of the time for the purpose of placing the matter in its true light before the House.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: On a question of privilege that might be done, but it would seem as if it would lead to a great deal of trouble and confusion if it were done on a specific motion in amendment such as this. I think the preferable course would be for the hon. member to take the matter up on some future occasion.

I shall take another opportunity then of placing the matter in its true light.

J, JACKSON (Selkirk). Mr.	
Speaker, before you	leave the chair, I wish
to rise to a question of veracity between the	
hon. member for	Marquette (Mr. W. J.
Roche) and myself	which arose yesterday.
That hon. gentleman made the statement	
that the polling subdivisions in Manitoba were made by the judges, and I denied the statement The hon. gentleman was appealing to the Prime Minister and he said :
I would remind him also that the present provincial polling subdivisions have been created by the judges-not by the Lieutenant Governor in Council nor by the returning officers, but by the judges. There can be no party advantage in arranging polling subdivisions; my objection is based upon the confusion likely to arise in having different polling subdivisions for the Domin'on from those established for the province.

In answer to that I said :
I may state, as the hon. gentleman (Mr. W. J. Roche) is not aware of it, that at present the j udges do not arrange the polling subdivisions, but the government arrange the registration districts and the polling divisions.
The hon. member for Marquette said iu reply :
As usual, the hon. gentleman is speaking without full knowledge when he says that the judges do pot fix the polling subdivisions.
1 would just like to point out to the hon. gentleman that in the Manitoba ' Gazette ' of April 28, 1906, there is a proclamation issued by the Lieutenant Governor, which reads as follows :
Whereas, pursuant to the provisions of the Manitoba Election Act, it is necessary to add to and revise the lists of electors in and for the several electoral divisions of the province of Manitoba, and it is necessary for the said purpose to issue a proclamation containing the information hereinafter set forth.
Now, therefore, we have thought fit and do hereby, pursuant to the powers and authority contained in the Manitoba Election Act, proclaim the following:
>1. That it has been determined to add to and revise the lists of electors for the several electoral divisions of the province, except those of Brandon City, Winnipeg Centre, Winnipeg North and Winnipeg South.
2. That the names and post office addresses of the persons appointed to act as registration clerks in the respective polling divisions of the several electoral divisions are as follows:
It goes on and gives the polling subdivisions for every electoral district in the province of Manitoba. Then it winds up by saying :
In testimony whereof we have caused these our letters to be made patent and the great seal of our said province of Manitoba to be hereunto affixed.
On the following page of the 'Gazette' you will find another proclamation :
Whereas it has been determined to add to and revise the list of electors in and for the several electoral divisions in the province of Manitoba, pursuant to the provisions of the Manitoba Election Act, and it is necessary for tbe said purpose to constitute the several judges of the county courts in the said province a board of registration;
Now, therefore, we have thought fit and do hereby, pursuant to the powers and authority contained in the Manitoba Election Act, con-situte the several judges of the county courts holding office in the province of Manitoba a board of registration for all and singular the premises.
I think it is not necessary for me to say anything further on this matter, except to ask the hon. member for Marquette how the judges can. obtain such knowledge of the various electoral districts as to enable them to lay out the polling subdivisions. As a practical politician, he knows that the mem-

bers always lay out the polling subdivisions. The judges would have to travel through every electoral district to get t!he necessary local knowledge to do the work. That is the political end of the business, and it is done by order of Lieutenant Governor in Council on the advice of the local member or the man who has been the candidate in the preceding election.

Nothing that the hon. gentleman has said has disproved in the slightest degree the statement I made. He asks what local knowledge the judges of the province of Manitoba have that they can lay out the polling' subdivisions ; and yet we approved yesterday of a section of an Act conferring that power on the judges.

They will have to
come to me for advice in regard to my district.

This is the reason the hon. gentleman has been bringing his influence to bear on the Prime Minister, in order that the judges might go to the member for Selkirk and get advice. Now the cat'is out of the bag. This is the influence behind the Throne. So that after all the judges are not going to lay out the polling subdivisions.
We will have to give them advice. You will have to give them advice too.

No, my advice will not be asked for. The hon. gentleman has read from the Manitoba * Gazette ' a proclamation defining the polling subdivisions, and he states .that orders in council are issued fixing the dates and places for the holding of the courts of revision. As a matter of fact the judges name the dates and places for the courts of revision and define the polling subdivisions. I have original letters from every judge of Manitoba showing that they fix the dates and places for the holding of courts of revision, as I stated yesterday. There is the order in council approving of every one of these recommendations and that was given out to the public by means of a proclamation, so that the judges in practice appoint the places and the very same practice and procedure is adopted in connection with the polling subdivision. The judges name the polling subdivisions and the Lieutenant Governor in council issues a proclamation making them known to the public.
Where did that emanate from?
If 'the hon. gentleman wants to read the information, I have it right in my possession now.
What is the use of looking to a judge against the statute?

I did not wish to place on ' Hansard ' those letters at this late stage, but, as the hon. gentleman seems in'doubt, I shall do so. Here is a letter from Mr. Justice Myers :
Winnipeg, April 7, 1908. James Hooper, Esq.,
Deputy Provincial Secretary, Winnipeg.
Dear Sir,-Replying to your letter of the 4th instant, I beg to say that the following times and places will suit me for holding the court of revision on the list of electors, namely:-
Lakeside at Macdonald, on Monday, June 8, from 11 o'clock, a.m., to 4 o'clock, p.m.; Gladstone at Gladstone, on Tuesday, June 9, from 1 o'clock, to 6 o'clock, p.m.; Beautiful Plains at Neepawa, on Wednesday, June 10, from 10 o'clock to 6 o'clock, p.m.
And so 'on, with each place an the riding. And these places named toy Judge Myers were in every instance adopted and a proclamation issued to the public.
Those are the courts of revision.

This letter is signed ' Yours sincerely, R. H. Myers,' who used to be the leader of the Liberals in the local legislature before he was made a judge. I have got letters from the other judges in other ridings naming the times and places for the holding of the courts.
Does the hon. gentleman argue that because the judges have named the places for registration they have also named the polling subdivisions?

I can give the very same evidence with regard to the polling subdivisions. They named the polling subdivisions as well. I also wish to inform the hon. gentleman that I have it on the authority of the King's Printer of Manitoba that the judges were not only asked to name the different places for the holding of courts of revision, but to delimit the boundaries of the polling subdivisions, and they did so, and that was approved by order in council and issued to the public in the form of a proclamation.

Before you leave the chair, Mr. Speaker. I wish to bring up for a few moments the matter of the damming of the St. Lawrence down at the Long Sault. I have in my hand a petition to the International Waterways Commission from parties representing the St. Lawrence Power Company, and it has reference to matters that ought to be brought before this House and country. The American company, called the Long Sault Development Company, and the St. Lawrence Company are iaentical in their interests. The one gets its powers from the Canadian and the other from the American authorities, but there can toe no

doubt that they have a community of interests. The American Power House and Lock Company, known as the Long Sault Development Company, proposeto construct a power house and lock between the foot of the Long Sault island and the main shore, as shown on plan No. 1. Permission has already been granted them by the New York State legislature, authorizing this construction so far as it lies in American territory. What particularly affects the Dominion of Canada is that they propose to dam the St. Lawrence main channel, as well as the south channel, so that virtually the whole river will be dammed at that point. In looking up the correspondence, I find that if they are allowed to do what they want, all the risk will be run by the Canadians and none at all by the Americans.	.
I wish to refer to another matter which ought to be brought to the attention of the House, and that is that the Waterways Commission, in their recommendations, seem to take a line which would permit or justify the Chicago canal. We know that is going to affect Lake Erie, because they are proposing, as a remedy for the damage that that work is likely to do to the navigation of Lake Erie, to dam the lake near the Niagara river. The several reports and data furnished by the commission point to tlie conclusion that for sanitary purposes the Chicago canal will necessarily be allowed. The Chicago people have put up the argument that it is altogether for drainage and sanitary purposes for the city of Chicago, but none the less it will affect navigation. If any of the reports can be relied on, it will lower the water, and I want to draw the attention of the government to this. In every instance in which this matter has been referred to any expert authority under the control of the government, the opinion is given that they have not sufficient data on which to base a judgment. Take all the reports and correspondence, and you will find that no one ventures to express an opinion as to what effect this1 will have on the navigation of the St. Lawrence. That is sufficient reason for our government to say at once that no such thing will be allowed.
Kefei ring again to the proposed damming of the St. Lawrence, when you look up the record you will see that this question was dealt with away back in 1842 by the Ashburton treaty. The seventh clause of that treaty distinctly states :
It is further agreed that the channel, in the river St. Lawrence on both sides of the Long Sault isla ids and- of Barnhart island

It refers to other rivers which I do not need to specify here.
-should be equally free and open to the ships, vessels and boats of both parties.

Now, away back as far as 1842-I suppose in part, for the reason that this place is very near the point where the river ceases to be the dividing line between the two countries-this matter was particularly referred to. We should stand on the principle of that treaty, we should maintain the spirit of that treaty, and keep both these channels open to both countries for all time. In the treaty of 1871. while not the same language is used, virtually the same conclusion is reached. And, while I am dealing with the matter. I think it well to state very clearly that the people along the river are very much concerned as to what may be done by the government. We have the assurance, given, I think, last February, by the right hon. Prime Minister that nothing would be done bv the government without all parties affected by such operations being consulted or notified. That is not the exact language, but that is the spirit of the promise given. This is a matter affecting the navigation of one of our greatest rivers, and it ought not to be dealt with in any serious way without the people's representatives in parliament being apprised of the conclusion that is come to. We know that if the people once get the privilege of dammiug that river, laying out millions of money as they propose to do according to their own statement, navigation will be but a secondary consideration with those who hold these great interests. I do not think the government should allow local commercial considerations to affect the navigation of a great river which has been made by solemn treaty, common to the two countries.
