When the House rose at six o'clock I was arguing that local commercial interests should not interfere with the navigation of a river that was of general importance. Now in order to give the House some idea as to what the St. Lawrence Power Company, in connection with the Long Sault Development Company, are asking the government of this country to do, I wish to read the request that they make upon our government :
(a)	To construct a solid masonry dam from a point near the Canadian main shore, about opposite lock 20, extending to the international boundary line, there to join a darn to be constructed in connection with the works above described in American territory.
(b)	To construct a power house between the northeasterly end of this dam and the Canadian shore, together with a new lock about 2,600 feet west of present lock 20, and an earthen dike, having a top width of about 100 feet, between this power house and lock, also a similar earthen dike extending from this lock northwesterly and parallel to the present

canal, and connecting with the main shore at Milles Roches.
(c)	To enlarge the present channel of Little river as above set forth, to a minimum width of about 800 feet, and to raise the level of the pond above the dams to an elevation five feet higher than the present level of the Cornwall canal above lock 20.
(d)	After the stability of all of the above described works has been satisfactorily proved, to remove the two earthen dams at the easterly and westerly ends of Sheik Island and to enlarge the present channel on the north side of Sheik Island.
And your petitioners as in duty bound will ever pray.
Now that is the proposition. That means to dam the St. Lawrence river at that point from the main shore over to meet similar works on the American side. I want to say this, that you cannot tell, in a work of that kind, what eventuality might arise. Something might occur that might change the whole aspect of that river so far as navigation is concerned, and if anything should occur to transfer the control of the navigation of that river now in our hands, to American control, in which the citizens of the United States were interested, then Canadian interests might suffer very materially. Now it may be quite a surprise to many in this country to learn that the people Sf Canada have not had the use of the New York state canals for thirty-seven years ; for thirty-seven years Canadian marine interests and Canadian vessels have not been allowed to use the New York State canals. Now what does that mean in case anything should be done to transfer the control of the navigation of the St. Lawrence at that point from the Canadian government to the American government ? As I say, you cannot tell what might happen. It is a peculiar circumstance, that while in the treaty of 1871 the United States government stipulated and agreed to urge upon the state of New York the wisdom of giving Canada the use of her canals, whether they carried out that obligation or not, the state of New York has not allowed Canadians to use their canals for the last thirty-seven years. If you go down into the Richelieu river you find that our pulp wood, our lumber and coal go down that river to Lake Champlain in American bottoms. These are things that ought to be considered, and I would like to consider them more at length if time allowed. I certainly think that this is a question deserving of careful consideration by the Canadian government; it is a question that should not be left to one or two men, but should be considered from the national standpoint of keeping that river for the use of Canadian navigation interests. That river is the channel through which imports from Europe are carried into the interior of this country, and it is the great navigable outlet to the sea in the summer time from the interior portion of Canada. It seems to
me the government cannot be too careful in dealing with those interests, because no engineer seems to be able to say what effect the damming of the river at that point, as proposed by these companies, might have on the navigation of the river. We know that the slowing of the current by ice jams some miles below Morrisburg has raised the river ten or twelve feet at Morrisburg. When the ice jams occur some eight miles below, the ice gradually fills in until you can drive across it at Morrisburg. This is the first time that it has been known to have reached as far up as Morrisburg. But it has occurred several times some miles below Morrisburg, and raised the water in the river several feet. If the proposed dams were built, the slowing of the current might bring on this ice jam and cause very serious injury to the people along the shores of the St. Lawrence on either side. There is this point to consider, that if you leave the river in its natural condition, any damage that may occur from ice jams, or from any natural cause, the government of this country could not be held responsible. But if we allow dams to be built across that river then this government would be responsible for damages that might result. I have felt it my duty, as voicing the feelings of my constituents along the river in that section of the country, to draw the attention of the House and the government to this important matter, and I regret that the time at our disposition will not allow me to pursue the subject further.

I did not think that this matter would come up for discussion at the present time. I may say that I have long taken a very keen interest in the development of power on the St. Lawrence river at or near the town of Cornwall. The hon. member for Dun-das (Mr. Broder) has expressed my sentiments when he says that the question of navigation is one of paramount importance, and if I considered for a moment that the accomplishment of this scheme would in any way injuriously affect the navigation of the St. Lawrence river, I would oppose it strenuously. But, Mr. Speaker, the matter is in that stage that I do not think this House is in a position intelligently to discuss it. The Canadian sections of the Deep Waterways Commission have given this matter a great deal of consideration, and in their report they express themselves as not yet having come to a conclusion, and they desire to get the very best expert engineering evidence before they finally report on the matter. I may say that the constituency which I have the honour to represent is vitally interested in this question.
We have had meetings of our town council and our board of trade and delegations have been sent to appear before the Deep Waterways Commission to urge upon them
1314V

that they give to this matter their most serious consideration. The Deep Waterways Commission have not acted hastily in this matter. They have held meetings at different times. They held a meeting in the city of Toronto and after they had had some representations against the scheme they, for the convenience of the people who might urge opposition to this scheme, adjourned their meeting to Montreal so as to give every one interested an opportunity of being heard. Not one engineer in this or any other country has put himself on record as saying that this scheme will injuriously affect navigation. On the other hand we have the reports of the most eminent American, Canadian and English engineers to the effect that this scheme would not only not injure navigation on the St. Lawrence, but would be of incalculable assistance to it. We saw what occurred here a few days ago. We have a canal, over 9 miles in length, some G or 7 miles of that canal are separated from the river by an earth embankment and a greater strain is being put upon the banks of this canal year by year by the increased size of the vessels. They are not increased in length because the locks will permit of a vessel of only a certain length passing through, but they have been increased in width and in carrying capacity. To-day we have vessels going through that canal carrying 80,000 and 90,000 bus.'hels of grain and with the increased displacement of water there is greater pressure put upon these banks. In 1903 I put myself on record in this House in favour of a lock at the foot of Sheik's Island dam, into the St Lawrence river. If that lock had been built, and engineers of that day. said it was quite feasible, we would have had no delay to vessels passing through the Cornwall canal. There would have been no request for a vote of $150,000 to repair break as it is very probable there would have been no break as vessels could have come down Sheik's Island dam, passed through that lock into the St. Lawrence and gone on- their way saving the time that it now takes to pass through five locks which is considerable, and saviag danger to banks of canal from large vessels passing through canal. My remarks at that time are to be found in ' Hansard ' of 1903, page 14137. I said : I
I understand from those who are engaged in navigation that a saving of an hour or two could be made by having a lock immediately east of the Sheik's island dam, which would let vessels into the St. Lawrence river without going down through three locks to the eastern end of the canal; and it would also permit all vessels to come up and enter the canal just at the foot of the dam and go through the Cornwall canal in a very short space of time. Vessel owners have told me that it would be an immense saving if that lock were put in, not only a saving of expense, but a great saving of time in passing through the canal.
Mr. PRINGLE
It would not have been a very expensive lock. It would have paid for itself between 1904 and the present time. That is practically the scheme now. The scheme to-day is to have a lock, or two locks, where this dam will be built so that vessels coming through Sheik's Island dam may pass on into the St. Lawrence, saving time and expense. This is a matter of the utmost importance to the whole surrounding country but it should not in any way influence myself or any man in this House in favour of this scheme if it is not practicable and if it is likely in any way to interfere with navigation. What are the objections we find ? My hon. friend has said that no engineer has been able to say what effect it would have on navigation. I ask my hon. friend to read the reports of the engineers who have investigated this matter most thoroughly and who say that the scheme would not be objectionable from the point of view of navigation but that on the other hand it would assist navigation.
There are one or two objections made with regard to this scheme. One is that it will prevent certain tourist steamers passing through the Long Sault rapids. I say at once that it will. For four months there are certain tourist steamers which pass down the Long Sault rapids. They say it will' destroy the scenic hffect. What does one eminent engineer say in regard to that ? He says :	' Take the great dam
on the Nile-I think it is called the Assouan dam ; that dam is bringing yearly increasing numbers of visitors to see its beauties. It is possibly the largest dam in the world.' When this dam is constructed on the St. Lawrence it will be the largest dam in the world and the beauty of the dam will be just as great as the beauty of the Long Sault rapids. But this is not the only rapid we have. There is a chain of rapids all down the St. Lawrence and many boats pass down through them to the city of Montreal. Now, it is said that it will back up the water on the property west of the Cornwall canal. What do the engineers say ? The engineers say that it will back up the water as far as Farran's Point canal and they say that in so far as Morrisburg is concerned the effect will be practically nothing, that it will be nil.
How many miles will that be ?

It will be 15 or 16 miles. There is a drop in the river from Morrisburg to where this dam would be erected of between 13 and 16 feet. We have between Morrisburg and the Long Sault a small rapid opposite Farran's Point and engineers say that it would practically do away with this rapid. It is a great inconvenience now to navigation and why ? Because steamers going west have to take to the Farran's Point canal instead of keeping to the river as they could not possibly

take their heavy loads up that raipd current. | This would do away with that inconvenience. The moment they came within the influence of this dam they would have practically smooth water until they got to Mor-risburg where they would take to the Mor-risburg canal. I ask the House to pardon me ; I know we are pressed very much for time, but this is a matter that could not be discussed intelligently in fifteen or twenty minutes. I have not taken up the time of this House for some time and it is a very important matter. For myself I do not see the necessity of it being brought ud at the present time because I am quite satisfied that the government would not consider entering into any arrangement for the construction of this dam until such time as they not only had a report from the Canadian section of the Waterways Commission, but until such time as they had brought the matter before this House where it could be very thoroughly discussed. My bon. friend has spoken of the channels. To-day all south of Barnhardt's island is the American channel which is practically the only navigable channel; 95 per cent of the water flows through that channel and only 5 per cent through what is an international channel, being the channel between Barnhardt's island and .the Canadian shore. The effect of the construction of this dain will be to send 50 per cent of the water to the Canadian side and 50 per cent to the American side. It is well to talk of the beauties of the St. Lawrence : nn one nnpi'e-ciates more than I do the grandeur of the Long Sault rapids, but I believe there will still be great beauty there after the construction of the dam and we will have hundreds of thousands of horse-power to be used by our people in manufacturing on the Canadian side. There will no doubt be a large development of power on the American side; they have it to-day. The Long Sault Power Company have their power at Messina. What has been the. result ? The construction of one of the greatest works in the United States. The Pittsburg Reduction Company have put up an enormous establishment there. They, came to us ; I went with them personally as I was anxious to see the work located on our side. They went over the St. Lawrence Power Company's scheme but found there was no possible way of getting more power than there is at the present without an enormous expense and they turned it down. They established their Canadian institution at Shaw-inigan Falls and built one of their American institutions right across from us. We wanted that industry and would have had it if we had the powers which we will have under this project. A great deal has been said by the lion, member for Grenville (Mr. J. D. Reid) against the St. Lawrence Power Company. It has been one of the best developments in eastern Ontario.
It has the largest rake-off of any company in Canada.

I do not know aything about the rake-offs, and I am not discussing the contract that has been threshed out before. It has been an enormous benefit. Only a few years ago one of our woollen mills closed down and had to go out of business. We were able to have it reopened because of the electrical power and to-day it is employing three or four hundred men in a different class of industry and owing to the power we have had other factories located there.
We suffer in Cornwall from floods in winter, caused by the frazil that comes down, forms in the rapids and passes under the ice which has become solid, causing a shove. The result has been that portions of the town have been flooded, and mills have been closed for weeks.' One of the largest of the cotton mills was flooded. These people are naturally interested in seeing this scheme go through, so long as it does not impair in any way the navigation of the Sit. Lawrence. They know from the engineers' reports that the result will be no floods in the winter. This water will be hemmed back, it will form almost level to the dam, will freeze solid there and there will be just a natural flow over the dam with no possibility of the injurious floods we have had in years past. On one occasion the government had to come to the rescue of people who had suffered from one of those heavy floods. It has been said that the American section of the International Waterways Commission nave reported favourably on this. If they have it has been after giving the matter the greatest possible consideration. When the Canadian section of the International Waterways Commission said to Mr. Calvin, to the Richelieu and Ontario Navigation Company and others who were opposing this scheme r Nominate an engineer and we will appoint him and get him to look into the matter and see what his report will be, they did not take the responsibility of nominating an engineer because no engineer would stand for the statements made by some of those people that the erection of this dam would decrease the flow of water east of Cornwall. Some went so far as to say it would affect the flow of water ait Montreal, but that statement was so ridiculous that they could not get any engineer to endorse it. The effect of this scheme would be that instead of only 5 per cent of the waters of the St. Lawrence going down on the Canadian side we would have 50 per cent. The effect, would be to give us all the power that could be developed, practically unlimited power, whereas we are now absolutely limited. It is no wonder that some of the power companies are instrumental in putting up opposition to this scheme. This development would be one

of tremendous advantage to the whole eastern portion of Ontario and I am satisfied it would be of great advantage to the county of Dundas, which my hon. friend (Mr. Broder) represents. While the Minister of Railways lias been expressing his opinion against this scheme it would tie a tremendous advantage to his own constituency for this power would be taken to Broeliville where it is needed, more than in any other town in Ontario. I have refrained from speaking on this before because I felt that we had not all the information before the House required for a full and intelligent discussion of the question, but when the hon. member for Dundas (Mr. Broder) opposes it in the dying days of the session, I feel that in the interests of the eastern portions of Ontario, especially in the interest of the county of Stormont, if this scheme does not injuriously affect navigation, but on the contrary, aids and assists it, the government should give it careful consideration and should procure all possible information on the subject before any agreement is entered into or any permission given for the erection of this dam. Of course 1 foresee that the permission would have to be a joint permission of the United States and Canada, but nothing T think should be done until the whole matter comes before parliament.

I protest absolutely' against the dam being built. It certainly would be unfair to have it built and destroy the navigation on the St. Lawrence. The hon. member for Cornwall (Mr. Pringle) complains that I have been finding-fault with the St. Lawrence Power Company. I have not been finding fault with them as a corporation, I have been criticising the agreement made by this government with the St. Lawrence Power Company for eighty-nine years, which . I think is' outrageous, while the price the government are paying this company is simply absurd. A scheme of this kind is such a great scheme, affecting the w-hole marine interests in this country, that I think no action should be taken by the government in regard to it until the whole matter is submitted to parliament. I only rose to ask if the Prime Minister can see his way to give us a promise that no action will be taken in the direction of granting a charter or the right to dam the River St. Lawrence until the matter is submitted to parliament and thoroughly discussed here. The right hon. gentleman did state a few months ago that nothing would be done until everv one had an opportunity of being heard; but I think we should have that opportunity in parliament, and if the Prime Minister would give us that promise, I do not think there will be any reason for detaining the House any longer at this time, as the matter could come up next session.

Being conversant with the territory covered by this discussion, Mr. PRINGLE.
there is a great temptation for me almost to attempt to make a speech; but I will resist the temptation. This is a matter that was brought before the department some months ago, and it was placed before members of the government-the premier, I think the Minister of Public Works, and myself. It is a matter of such great importance that it could not be dealt with quickly or without the gravest consideration. The government feeling that it affected particularly three departments-the Marine Department, the Public Works Department and the Railways and Canals Department-appointed a chief engineer of each of those departments, and these three form a committee, as it were, to-look into the matter from the departmental standpoint. They have not yet submitted to their respective departments the result of their investigation; they have not yet had time to do so. But, to be very brief, the matter is of such great importance-and there are two sides to it-that before anything could be done it would require the best consideration of the best talent that could be brought to bear upon it. The government has no idea of taking any steps to commit the country to anything in connection with this scheme until parliament has a full opportunity to discuss it and approve or disapprove of it.

To provide for the appointment of a post office inspector, an assistant inspector and three clerks at North Bay, Ontario, $5,000.
Will there be an office there for the staff?
Yes.
Who is to occupy the position of additional post office inspector for New Brunswick?
That is a matter of promotion, and we have not yet decided, but will in a few days.
Has the hon. gentleman filled the place of the late Mr. Ryan?
We shall in a few days. Mr. Gross, the senior officer, and an old and faithful employee, will be given the appointment.
ItEID. I thought I saw that Mr. Hawken is going to be superannuated.
Yes ; he was appointed before confederation, and has on many occasions applied for superannuation, tie has done very faithful service, but of late the office has been rather in want of a younger man.

I have a letter from a constituent of mine who is a mail carrier and has not received justice at the hands of the department. I refer to Mr. Gibbons, who has a claim some three years old. He had a mail contract and he went to Clifton, some ten or fourteen miles further than his contract called for. He sent in a claim for something over $100 and the department offered him $28, which he indignantly refused.
I urged his claim on my hon. colleague's predecessor very strongly some time ago.
This matter has been before the department some time. I am afraid the Minister of Public Works could not have urged it with his usual vigour, or it would have been paid long ago.
I pleaded very strongly.

I am satisfied that if the facts were put before the Postmaster General he would recognize the justice of the claim. A department with a constantly inci'easlng surplus does not want to get services for nothing.
If my hon. friend will send in this claim I shall give it every consideration.
What progress is the hon. minister making towards the establishment of a post office at St. Charles? The people are extremely anxious to have one, and write me frequently about it.

Some weeks ago I established a post office at the request of the people of the locality, selecting what I thought the best site, near the church. But I have received a complaint from some petitioners who say that this is not the proper site. There is a difference of
opinion among the people on this point. I have written to the inspector, Mr. McLeod, at Winnipeg, asking him to make a choice of a site.
It will depend on the inspector ?
Yes, he will make the selection.

I have found the letter of which I was speaking. The writer says :
They made me carry the daily for a month from Clifton, also the Long's cove bag for a time. And about three years ago the inspector had a bill made for me of $111.43.
The inspector is Mr. Colter, of St. John.
I was not quite satisfied and wanted $124, and sent this bill to the Deputy Postmaster General, but have heard nothing of it since.
Perhaps this was sent at a time when the Deputy Postmaster General was away. He was absent on leave for four months. I will see that the papers are brought before me and that justice !s done.
Does that mean that you will send the cheque in the moi mug ?
Practically so, if the claim is a valid one.
Has the department come to a decision respecting the establishment of a post office at Graham Station ?

I have asked the inspector to give me a fresh report, as there are conflicting statements with regard to that post office. I am sure that the distance justifies placing a post office at that point, but I will act on the report of the inspector.
Does not the department issue a monthly circular showing the new post offices established during the month and the changes made in existing offices ?
Yes.
Why is it not sent to members of this House ? I am sure it is information that would be of use to them.
I will see that that is done.' [DOT]

At Barrie, there are two post offices, one in the old part of the town and one at Aliandale, known as Allandaie post office. I understand that letters transmitted from one post office to the other must bear a two-cent stamp. I called the Postmaster General's attention to this some time ago and, as I recollect it, he said the matter would be adjusted when the Bill went though. I have a letter which I have forwarded to the Postmaster General from a constituent of mine, not a political supjxo*[DOT]-ter I am sorry to say. who asked me to in quire into the matter. He says that the postmaster at Barrie informs him that he

has no instructions on the subject, and the two-cent rate is still charged.

The one-cent drop letter rate will come into effect as soon as the Bill is sanctioned.
Miscellaneous-amount required co piy losses sustained by Chinese residents of Vancouver in connection with the riots of Vancouver in September, 1907, and the legal expenses arising out of the inquiry into the same, $26,990.
Mr. BERGERON'. Are we to expose ourselves to such damages every time there is a row between whites and the Chinese in Vancouver ?
It has Deen a good lesson, and I hope it will be the last.
How much are the legal expenses ?
About $1,000.
Is not this a municipal matter ? If there were a riot in Ottawa or Montreal, would not the municipality have to pay the damage ?

There is a difference in this case. I do not wish to excuse the acts perpetrated in September last, but my hon. friend will understand that this is quite different from a riot taking place, say, in Ottawa, where there is only one nationality -that is, we are all Canadians. But this riot in Vancouver was engineered, I am sorry to say, not by our own people, but by foreigners

Mr. SAM, HUGHES. Galvanized Yankees.
Mr. LEMIEUX 

and directed against
other foreigners. They have appealed to their respective governments for redress and payment of the losses that have been suffered. We thought, under the circumstances, the government should see that this amount was paid, I hope we shall not hem any more of such riots.
Are we paying for houses wrecked, glass broken and that kind of thing ?

If the hon. gentleman (Mr. Bergeron) will refer to the report 1 laid on the table some time ago, first as to the Chinese claims, then as to the Japanese claims, he will see that the whole matter was sifted to the bottom. Mr. King went to Vancouver and took evidence. He had ,an attorney there to represent the government, and there were legal representatives of the Chinese and Japanese governments. No fancy damages are to be paid or were paid.	[DOT]
No doubt about that; but if these people enjoy this sport and go in for another row, will the government of Canada have to pay for the pots cassfis ?
I think we must regard this case as exceptional.
Does not the head tax paid by the Chinese go to the Receiver General ?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Only half of it; the other half goes to the provincial government.
I was going to say that if the government receives the head tax it is only reasonable they should pay the damages.

If this government is taxing Chinese who come in $500 a head, will he undertake to tax these galvanized Yankees, these anarchists who come in, $500 a head ?

Has this commission succeeded in connecting Mr. W. T. R. Preston With the inducing of these oriental immigrants to come to Canada ?

I am glad to be in a position to assure my hon. friend (Mr. Sam. Hughes) that Mr. Preston has nothing to do with the influx of orientals into Canada. Quite the contrary. I met Mr. Preston when in Japan, and I am in a position to say he is rendering very valuable service to this country on this question as well as in relation to commerce. He is a good and very efficient officer of the government.
To provide for expenses of Royal Commission appointed to inquire into the industrial disputes in connection with the cotton industry in the province of Quebec, $2,000.
What has the commission to do? Would my hon. friend tell us how It is going to work?

The commission has begun its sittings in Montreal to-day, as I see by the Montreal 'Star,' and several witneses have been summoned, and Mr. King is hearing evidence. My hon, friend will remember under what circumstances this eommis-

sion was appointed. During the month of May, a strike occurred at several points in the province of Quebec, at Montmorency, at Yalleyfield in the county represented by my hon. friend, at Magog and in Montreal. I was asked as Minister of Labour to intervene between the mill owners and their operatives. All I did was to promise the men that if they would return to work and accept the sataus quo I would appoint a commission. They said :	We do not know
what to do. One month we are told that our salaries are cut down by 10 per cent, and we do not know whether the financial position of the cotton industry is such as to justify a reduction in our salaries, therefore we ask the government to appoint a commission to investigate the circumstances. I did not make any promise, but I returned to Ottawa and submitted the case to the cabinet, and it was decided to appoint Mr. Mackenzie King, who has had large experience in these matters, to hold an investigation. He will confine his activities to the province of Quebec, and will ascertain whether it is true that the salaries have been necessarily reduced on account of over production, as it is claimed.
Several delegates from the cotton workers met the hon. gentleman in Montreal, I believe. What did they say to him, and what answer did he give them?

I do not exactly remember the answer I gave. But they represented to me that they lhad suffered two reductions in wages within the last five or six months, ten per cent one time, and ten per cent at another time, and they gave me the facts and figures. They showed that the average wages paid to men in Montreal was $10 or $11 per week, including men, women and children. I thought that was not a very high wage in these prosperous times. They said that there were some people working in those factories, even some mechanics, who were only receiving $5 a week. The delegates represented about 5,000 working people, and they said they would accept the conditions offered by the mills and return to work provided the government would appoint a commission to investigate the situation, and see whether it was true that the cotton market was glutted with goods, and that the owners were justified in reducing their wages in consequence.

What kind of an investigation is Mr. King holding? Some time ago I remember my hon. friend saying that Mr. King, or some other commissioner, would ask the company to show their books and to reveal the stocks they had on hand, and generally the financial condition of the company, and whether they were in a position to pay higher wages to their operatives. I told my hon. friend that I did not think the commissioner could force the company to show their books, and I am under the same
impression still. I would ask my hon. friend to say how Mr. King can force any one of those companies to bring forward their nooks and show whether, from the condition of their business, they are able to pay the higher wages that they have so far refused to pay.

They will not be bound to pay higher wages, even if it is proven by their books that they have the means to do so, but the investigation will allow the public to judge who is right and who is wrong. The !hon. gentleman questions Mr. King's power to examine the books. I think he is mistaken, because Mr. King is appointed under the Great Seal, he has a, royal commission, and it gives him power to investigate the books of the company.

Does Mr. King's commission empower him to inquire into the relationship existing between the cotton industry here in Canada and that industry in other countries, and to consider whether the Canadian tariff is high enough to protect these industries? Perhaps the Minister of Finance could answer that question. Has Mr. King power to investigate the effect of the tariff upon Canadian industries ?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: No, I should say not.
That is the whole question.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: That is a matter of opinion, some people think it is not.

I believe that there is something wrong in the present condition of the cotton industry. I am better acquainted with that than with the woollen industry, although I know that in my county the woollen industry is closing down this week, and will not resume unless there is a change in the tariff. But the cotton industry has been a subject for politicians to make capital out of. A man by the name of Paquette is playing a great game in Montreal to help the Liberal party. He has become one of the leaders of tbe workingmen, and has got them to believe that he is a very powerful man. But he made a mistake the last time because he thought the elections would take place in the fall. He was foiled in his attempt at that time; though he succeeded once before, when I was the victim. The workingmen were deceived, I was defeated and another man gained the seat. Now this is what I wish to bring to the attention of the House. On the last occasion only a few men went on strike, the mule spinners I believe they are called, who furnish work to the great body of the other workers in the mills, and when the mill spinners strike there is nothing for the other operatives to do. But the other operatives were not quite ready to follow their example, they became frightened. The manager of the mills had told them in a very candid manner that he could not pay them the wages which they

had been receiving. I may say that a year ago this man Paquette brought on a strike just at the time that the mills were in need of their men, they had orders from the west to fill, and they were caught by the throat, and had to give a 20 per cent increase of salary. But a change took place, orders were cancelled all over Canada, and then the manufacturers told their men in a very honest way that they could not continue paying the same salaries and keep their mills running, that they could only keep their mills running on condition of a reduction of 10 per cent in wages. Well, the men did not believe that, the agitators told them that it was not true. So when the mule spinners did go on strike, about one hundred of them, the mills were closed down, and the men were thrown out of work. There was an over production of goods, the stores were filled with merchandise, orders were cancelled, and the strike could not have occurred at a more convenient time for the employers. This took place during the last local elections. Now what I complain of is that Liberal politicians are responsible for this trouble, and the Minister of Labour is responsible.
The Minister of Labour gave these men to understand that they would appoint a royal commission, that that commission would settle matters, that it would go to the factory and find out, by looking at their books, if the company were in a jiosition to pay the workingmen what they were asking or not. That was very unfortunate. My hon. friend knows that the Investigation Act passed last year gives him authority to compel public utilities to disclose tLeir affairs, but that he has no right to go to a private concern and ask them to open their books to him. These men relied upon the statement of my hon. friend that he would do something 'for their relief, and they did not go back to work for nearly three weeks, involving a loss of about $150,000 in wages and otherwise. When I saw the appointment of the royal commission published in the papers, it struck me that it would be of no use. Mr. King, whether he is appointed under the Great Seal, or twenty Great Seals, could not, under the law, force any company to show their books if they refused to do so. We should be honest about this. What the cotton and woollen industries are complaining of is the tariff. My hon. friend (Mr. Fielding) knows very well that there are gentlemen sitting behind him who have been for the last ten days worrying him to do something with respect to the tariff. About $14,000,000 worth of cottons and about $10,000,000 worth of woollens come in to compete with the workingmen of Canada. You may appoint all the commissioners you like, you may drag the Great Seal from one end of Canada to the other, but until you give protection to these industries they cannot compete with the product of Mr. BERGERON.
foreign workmen. You cannot pay a man $2 a day to make cotton and expect him to compete with a man in England who will work for 00 cents a day. Moreover, we give a preference to induce manufacturers in Great Britain to send cotton into this market. These factories in Canada to-day are working just on tolerance. At any moment they may close their doors, because they are not making any money. We cannot expect people to put their money into industries only to lose it. It is a matter of tariff and nothing else, and the appointment of this royal commission is only throwing dust in the eyes of these workingmen. It would have been better if the minister had gone to them and said : We cannot do anything for you ; you will have to go to your employers and leave it to them ; if they are in a position to pay you more wages they will, and if they are not we cannot help it.

Of course, I am not going to discuss the question of protection, it is late in the session to take up tariff matters. If, as the hon. gentleman says, this commission has been a sham to throw dust in the eyes of the public, I could have appointed it during the local campaign in May. But I did not do so. It is my duty as Minister of Labour to adjust any differences that may exist between capital and labour, and powers are conferred for that purpose upon the Minister of Labour by the Act. Yes, it is my duty to see that differences are adjusted between capital and labour. Here, in the case, were 0.000 men parading the streets of Montreal, Yalley-field, Magog and near the city of Quebec, and they were complaining bitterly that they could not stand the reduction which was imposed, that the reduction was too severe. I sasr ' imposed ' ; I do not know if circumstances imposed that reduction upon them or not.
If the manufacturers cannot pay them any more, what are you going to do about it?
I heard their side of the story. I heard from Mr. Gordon, of Montreal, and I saw Mr. Simpson in Val-leyfield.
Tell us what they said?

They said it was a question of tariff. But still the operatives retorted :	They cut down our wages and
they continue paying the same dividends, and in s.ome cases pay increased dividends. I am not saying that statement is true. I have not ascertained for myself, except in a general way. But, Sir, as Minister of Labour was it not my duty to say to these 6,000 men parading the streets : Return to your work ; you have not the means to remain on strike. I advised them, in a fatherly way, to return to work so as to help their

families. They promised me that t!hey would return to work provided an independent commission was appointed to investigate the differences between themselves and their employers. The commission has been appointed. No man is better equipped to conduct such an investigation than the Deputy Minister of Labour, Mr. King. He is now proceeding with the work, and we will see what his report is.
Some lion. MEMBERS. Carried.
My hon. friend says that he met these men, and that he told them in a fatherly way to return to work and he would see that a royal commission was appointed.
Yes.
The royal commission was not appointed, and as a consequence of that they did not go back.
The commission was appointed.
Not at that time.
Mr. King was away.
But I understand that my hon. friend says that he could have appointed somebody else.
Yes.

And nobody else was appointed at the time ; the consequence was that these men remained out of the mills when they would have gone back to work. They waited until they were starving, and they do not believe any more in the promises of the hon. gentleman, or in what is told them by agitators who, if they went to Valleyfield, would be thrown into the water. They have gone back to work : they could not get anything to eat in the butchers' or grocers' shops, but they went back to the mills and begged to be given work. They are out of the union to-day, and I pity the man who goes there to advise them to go into a union after this. They said : We want to work ; we do not want to starve. The manager said : I will give you work at the rate of pay that I can afford to give you. My hon. friend says that these cotton companies are continuing to pay dividends. These men cannot put their money into these industries as a matter of public charity. They go into them with the idea of making money, and it is a good thing that they should make money. When they erect buildings like those which they have erected in Valleyfield, at a cost of $3,000,000. they do not do it for public charity, nor for their health but to make money, and if they do not make money they cannot employ
3.000	or 4.000 men. Mr. Simpson, of the Valleyfield mills, said to them : ' I will pay you as much as I can afford to ; later on, if I can afford to do so, I will increase your wages.' We know that to-day, under this
government, it costs the workingman 50 or 00 per cent more to live. The workingman who got $1.50 a day before this government came into power could live better than he can to-day at $2 a day. The crux of the whole situation is the tariff, and it would be a great deal better to say so instead of pursuing the course which the hon. minister has in appointing this royal commission. The Minister of Finance knows that there are lots of men in this House sitting behind him who are asking him to-day to do something with the tariff with regard to cotton and woollen_ goods, and, if that is so, there is no use trying to deceive us. These industries, cotton and woollen, cannot continue in a prosperous condition in Canada.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: It may be well for my hon. friend to include in his statement to his friends in Valleyfield, that just across the border in the United States, where they have the blessing, if it be a blessing, of a much higher tariff than we have, the paralysis of the cotton industry was worse than in Canada.

I will not deny that but the circumstances are entirely different and my hon. friend knows, or if not he should know, that if we had not imported $14,000,000 worth of cottons and if they had been made in this country these working men would be continuing to work at the rates of two years ago.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General

We do not know whether the oil-bearing formation will be found on the island or not; but experts in well boring, better experts than my hon. friend, have given us estimates of the probable cost of this work. tic for the welfare of the Indians, will he able to do great public service. The Minister of the Interior has mentioned Father Ryan as the gentleman whom he has in mind for this position. I know Father Ryan and I am sure that his work

(Translation.) Mr. Speaker, with your leave, I think I should give a few explanations as regards the manner in which the public funds have been expended in the constituency which I represent here. I regret I am not in a position to present these with as much ease in English as in French, and for the sake of clearness and brevity, I shall take advantage of the right I enjoy of expressing in my native tongue.
My hon. friend from Kings and Albert (Mr. Fowler) has assumed the task of arraigning the government in consequence of certain works which have been carried out, with the consent of the minister, such as bridges, repairs to telegraph lines, the latter having been built through my district in the public interest, and not at all for local purposes.
I have the honour to represent here a constituency of exceptional importance and extent. The greater part of the north shore of the St. Lawrence lies within my county. For the purpose of assisting navigation. the government built a telegraph line along that coast. That line is entirely for the benefit of the country as a whole, and not for that of the residents in my constituency. It so happens that along that telegraph line there are small groups of

population, small villages, at certain places, inhabited by fishermen, or by both fishermen and farmers ; but in the majority of cases there are no municipalities in existence. In other parts, In order to enable people to vote, municipalities have been organized, the valuation of which is very small. That telegraph line was built without foresight or care; it was practically forced on the people against their will. The posts were set in spite of provincial and federal legislations, and each post which was put inside of the road ditch was an impediment to travel. That work was done at the time the friends of the hon. member for Kings and Albert were in power. I mean the work which was carried on between 1880 and 1890, previous to my occupying a seat in this House ; and to-day, the government and your humble servant are called upon in honour and conscience to mend past errors, inasmuch as the law and common sense will allow. And now, my hon. friend, not knowing who are the people moving him in the matter, comes out with this unfair criticism and compels the people concerned to put matters in their true light, through my voice, and to place the responsibility where it belongs.
I regret that my hon. friend does not understand what I am saying, but having the right to speak in French, I want to prove to the government and to the Minister of Public Works, that this whole investigation that has been going on in the Public Accounts Committee, through the efforts of my hon. friend from St. Antoine (Mr. Ames), has no real foundation, but rests merely on the machinations of a group of local politicians, so-called Liberals or Tories, who really belong to neither party.' A small ring of speculators in my county have supplied the hon. member for St. Antoine with the information on which he has based his charges, being unaware that such information has no foundation in fact, is untrue and unfair, and the member for St. Antoine, in turn, has passed on this information to the member for Kings and Albert, who has very cleverly brought it once more before the House. However, he did not really know what he was talking about, being content with to repeat here strings of stories of which he would never have spoken, had he taken the pains of verifying the statements; for then he would have known that he had no interest in repeating stories like these, which finally fall back on his friends.
About forty years ago, the Canadian government thought fit, and rightly so, to build a telegraph line from Bay St. Paul, in the county of Charlevoix, to the city of Chicoutimi, in the county of Chicoutimi and Saguenay, with a view to providing the people of that district, which was then very much out of the way, the benefit of an up-to-date means of communication. For that
purpose, advantage was taken of the road which the local government had opened through the Laurentian hills, between St. Urbain and St. Alexis. That road, as soon as the Quebec and Lake St. John Railway had reached Chicoutimi, was given up by the local government, and since then, the Dominion government, in order to protect their rights as to the telegraph line just referred to, was, and is still, obliged to repair that road for purposes of maintenance.
Eighteen miles from the parish of St. Alexis is the township of Ferland, where a small group of settlers have located under favourable conditions. On account of the remoteness of their location, they have, through me, applied to the Minister of Public Works requesting him to be so kind as to allow them to connect, on the main line running from Bay St. Paul to Chicoutimi, what I might call a side line, about two miles long, which would enable them to communicate more easily with the rest of the world. That application was immediately granted with pleasure, the expenditure called for being very small and the service thus rendered to settlers in my district being of great value to them. Now, having found this out,-although I see here nothing that should not be highly commended, my hon. friend from St. Antoine, the other day, before the Public Accounts Committee, flushed with virtuous indignation and gave an exhibition of himself which hon. members then present will loug remember. The settlers concerned, to whose knowledge will be brought the facts which I am stating to-night, would gladly listen to my hon. friend's argument, if he were so kind as to come and point out to them wherein there is a scandal or a waste of money in connection with work.
The bridge on the Cedar river referred to by the hon. member is situated in that, part of the road I have just spoken about, and, consequently, forms part of the maintenance of the telegraph line. Further west, is the swamp to which the hon. member for Kings and Albert has referred, on the road between St. Alphonse and Chicoutimi, and where he has also discovered some sort of scandal. Let me tell him that if, while building that line,' his friends, instead of putting the telegraph posts inside the road ditch, had put them, as the law required, in the proper spot, outside the ditch, there would have been no necessity for his informers to maliciously use him as an instrument for misleading public opinion and unfairly criticising the government. After all, that is only a mere business proposition which was carefully considered by the officers of the department and the council of St. Alphonse, the latter, in consequence of the trouble and damages inflicted by the improper building of the

line, claiming from the government the compensation to which they were entitled, or else the removal of the line. All parties concerned have accepted as equitable the settlement now proposed, which is one of the most practical and acceptable which the government could make under the circumstances.
Reference has been made by my lion, friend to a bridge at l'Anse St. Jean, which he managed to mix up with a school-house matter, and stated, in support of his contention, that the bridge had no connection whatever with the telegraph line. I am willing to pay the expenses of my hon. friend if he will visit the spot, so that he may be in a position to judge of the fairness of his informers; and he will find out that the bridge referred to is right in front of the telegraph office of the parish, and facing the house of the man employed to repair the line between l'Anse it Cheval and St. Alexis. He will also find out that with a paltry $200, the amount voted for that purpose, it would have been impossible, in the ordinary course, to build a bridge 200 feet long, suitable for general traffic. I hope the hon. gentleman will not press the point of order, because the hon. member for King's and Albert (Mr. Fowler) went out of his way to make an attack on the hon. member for Chicoutimi (Mr. Girard) in regard to the expenditure of public money in his county. I think the hon. member for Chicoutimi should have an opportunity to reply.
I did not go out of my way to make an attack on anybody. I merely read statements and gave facts.
You must take the responsibility of your statements.

An arrangement has been made between the two sides of the House to bring this session to a close on Saturday. If my hon. friend does not want to carry out that arrangement, this side is willing to stay here until next week or next month.

Will the hon. gentleman say that after the member for Kings and Albert, at this late stage of the session and the night, made the attack he did with regard to expenditures in Chicoutimi, the hon. member for that county should not be allowed to reply ?
Certainly, let him reply as long as he likes.

The hon. gentleman from that county has already occupied more time in the reply than my hon. friend from Kings and Albert did in his statement. I was a party to the arrangement made last night, that in the time allotted to this subject we were to have practically the whole time. That arrangement is now broken.

I did not like to break any arrangement that has been made, but the hon. member for Kings and Albert has been dealing with so many things in my own riding that I think I should be allowed to answer him.
Go on.

I regret Mr. Speaker, I have spoken at such length. My hon. friend from Kings and Albert has compelled me to do so. I thought I had the right to answer every one of his charges. I wish to repeat what I said a moment ago, that the Conservative party of the district have not approached the opposition in the person of Simon Lapointe, who came to Ottawa to meet I know not whom. He may represent and belong to a certain class of Conservative parasites who associate with a small number of Liberal people of the same kind, whose existence in the county, unfortunately, we cannot avoid admitting. But I repeat it, the Conservative party in the county has not used this gentleman as its spokesman; and the government may rest assured of one thing, which I am anxi-

ous to impress on the mind of my hearers, and it is this: In Imy district we are new, we are poor, we are needy, but the majority of us are not looking for honours, because we have been brought up in an environment where honour is not a matter of jest; and no one would dare in our midst to try and knife whomever had extended a helping hand to him, whomever had been of service to him, be it the government or be it an individual, should he be a Liberal or should he be a Conservative. We are proud of our education, we glory in it fit may not give as brilliant results, but it is nobler, grander, better.
In our midst there is no Chateau-Sague-nay paid ten cents on the dollar, nor people paying their debts with worthless cheques; we make it a point to brand the few amongst us who act otherwise.
1 am not ashamed of what I have done for my county. I glory at the thought, and my mindi is quite made up to persevere. Always and everywhere have I acted toward the government and my constituents loyally and honorably. The government have not to regret what they have done. Far from it, the people concerned will seize the first opportunity of showing their gratitude. In the future the government should do as iu the past, and those who are trying to hurt the government in these parts of the country where those questions are not well understood, will not get much benefit from it. if they only have courage enough to say publicly what was said by the honorable member for Grenville (Mr. J. D. Reid). He said before the Committee of Public Accounts, after becoming acquainted with the charges made: ' That is too small for me.' Such is the verdict of an impartial member of this House, who had followed the trial, and it absolutely exonerates the government, its officers and myself, and we have reason to be proud of such a verdict.

Notwithstanding the lateness of the hour. I propose to place on ' Hansard ' the facts of the case. For many years the federal government have been constructing federal lines of telegraph in the eastern portion of the province of Quebec known as the Chicoutimi district. Some weeks ago the papers regarding payments in the Auditor General's Report were ordered by the Public Accounts Committee, and Mr. Tache, the chief engineer of the Public Works Department, was brought here and was examined by the hon. member for St. Antoine (Mr. Ames) for nearly two hours, and by other members. He was examined about every item in the Auditor General's Report regarding the payments of money over these telegraph lines, he was examined about roads and bridges, and he stated- emphatically that not one dollar of that money had been spent for any other purpose except purposes in connection with the telegraph lines.

He said that in certain places they had built a bridge which was used by children going from one portion of the village to another, but he said that by building that bridge they saved four or five miles in going around to repair the telegraph lines, and that it was absolutely necessary. He stated that in one or two places there were long distances without a single settler, and that they had to repair these roads in order to get along so as to repair the telegraph lines. And some person, I presume the hon. member for St. Antoine (Mr. Ames), has prepared a statement absolutely at variance with the facts as given before the Public Accounts Committee. There is not one word of truth in that statement. That is a pretty strong statement for me to make, but I make it deliberately. And the hon. member for Kings and Albert (Mr. Fowler) is the honourable medium by which that dishonest statement is placed on the records of this House.
Hear, hear.

That calls forth applause from hon. members opposite-not because they understand what they are applauding but simply because it is a sweeping statement made by one on their own side. The hon. gentleman (Mr. Carvell) is a lawyer, and he ought to know that he is not warranted in making the statement that there is not one word of truth in the statements that I have read
Not a word is true according to the evidence before the Public Accounts Committee.

So far as personal knowledge is concerned the hon. member (Mr. Carvell) has absolutely no acquaintance with the facts ; he has never been in the place, never saw one of these bridges or the telegraph lines. He is taking his story from what some one else has said, whether on oath or not is another matter. He says that in all I have said there is not a word of truth. The evidence of which the hon. gentleman speaks related to the telegraph line and the bridges built supposedly in connection with it. But I took up other matters. And yet the hon. gentleman, without knowledge, without having heard any sworn testimony with regard to these matters, makes the sweeping statement that the whole thing is untrue. That of course, is to be expected from the hon. gentleman-and he is the honourable medium by which that honourable statement is made to this honourable House, to use his own phrase.

Mr. OLIVER moved that the following be inserted as subsection 2 and 3 of section 123.
2.	Grain which is shipped from points west of Winnipeg to Winnipeg for orders, as provided in section 99c of the Manitoba Grain Act, and which goes forward without delivery in Winnipeg, shall be inspected at Winnipeg amd the certificate of inspection shall be issued at the end of 'the period of detention: provided, however, that on the written order of the agent of the shipper a oar of grain held at Winnipeg shall he inspected on its arrival and the certificate of inspection issued.

maintopic: MANITOBA GRAIN ACT-INSPECTION AND SALE OF GRAIN.
speechtext: Will the minister explain that?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: MANITOBA GRAIN ACT-INSPECTION AND SALE OF GRAIN.
speechtext:
Tbe first of the two subsections provides that grain which is being held at Winnipeg for orders shall be inspected at the end of the period of detention. If tbe car has been held the inspection shall be made when it is going out and not immediately after it has come in except that the
shipper may order it inspected after it comes in. If be does not so order it is inspected as it goes out.
Mr. SCHAFFNER, Why on going out ?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: MANITOBA GRAIN ACT-INSPECTION AND SALE OF GRAIN.
speechtext: It is necessary to inspect it at some time and if it is to be sold on sample it is not desirable to inspect it before the sale is made; but if it is not sold in Winnipeg it is necessary that the inspection shall be made before it goes east from Winnipeg in order that no grain may go east from Winnipeg except under Inspection.

maintopic: MANITOBA GRAIN ACT-INSPECTION AND SALE OF GRAIN.
speechtext: Would it interfere with the sample market to have the inspection before the grain goes on the sample board?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: MANITOBA GRAIN ACT-INSPECTION AND SALE OF GRAIN.
speechtext: It was thought that if it had been already inspected and the certificate issued the grain would be ticketed as of a certain grade, tbe buyer would buy on that grade and much of the advantage of the sample market would be lost.

maintopic: MANITOBA GRAIN ACT-INSPECTION AND SALE OF GRAIN.
speechtext: Is this the only clause in the Bill providing for a sample market?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: MANITOBA GRAIN ACT-INSPECTION AND SALE OF GRAIN.
speechtext: The only provision.

maintopic: MANITOBA GRAIN ACT-INSPECTION AND SALE OF GRAIN.
speechtext: How does this compare with the sample market, say in Minneapolis?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: MANITOBA GRAIN ACT-INSPECTION AND SALE OF GRAIN.
speechtext: The cases are not parallel. Winnipeg is on the direct route to the head of the lake.

maintopic: MANITOBA GRAIN ACT-INSPECTION AND SALE OF GRAIN.
speechtext: The owner of a mixing elevator in Winnipeg can buy grain, mix It as he sees fit, put it on track, call for inspection and forward the grain on that inspection.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: MANITOBA GRAIN ACT-INSPECTION AND SALE OF GRAIN.
speechtext: Yes.

maintopic: MANITOBA GRAIN ACT-INSPECTION AND SALE OF GRAIN.
speechtext: Does he not think that is throwing the door open towards the mixing of grain and losing the identity of our wheat in its shipment to the foreign market. I do not think this meets the wishes of the Grain Growers' Associations.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: MANITOBA GRAIN ACT-INSPECTION AND SALE OF GRAIN.
speechtext: There is undoubtedly every objection to the mixing of grain once it has been graded, but there can be no objection to mixing before the grain is assembled at the point of inspection. If we can guarantee that from the point of assemblage and inspection forward there shall be no mixing we will have achieved the purpose in the mind of every western man interested in this trade. There must be some point at which the grain trade changes from sample to grade and it is generally conceded that the point should be Winnipeg.

maintopic: MANITOBA GRAIN ACT-INSPECTION AND SALE OF GRAIN.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: MANITOBA GRAIN ACT-INSPECTION AND SALE OF GRAIN.
speechtext: No, that grain is sampled for inspection at Emerson.

maintopic: MANITOBA GRAIN ACT-INSPECTION AND SALE OF GRAIN.
speechtext: I suppose a mixing elevator could be established at Emerson, and that eventually a sample market could be established there the same as in Winnipeg.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: MANITOBA GRAIN ACT-INSPECTION AND SALE OF GRAIN.
speechtext: Of course the sample market is of no value unless there is a large number of samples and a large number of buyers. One of the difficulties about the sample market at Winnipeg is that there may not be enough sample buyers to make the proposition successful.

maintopic: MANITOBA GRAIN ACT-INSPECTION AND SALE OF GRAIN.
speechtext: Suppose that somebody thinks that it is to his material advantage to erect an elevator and go into the mixing business and establish a sample market, does this Act restrict any such operation?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: MANITOBA GRAIN ACT-INSPECTION AND SALE OF GRAIN.
speechtext: No ; there is nothing against it.

maintopic: MANITOBA GRAIN ACT-INSPECTION AND SALE OF GRAIN.
speechtext: Does the minister think that the sample market will be of any advantage to the farmers, restricted, as it is, to the period after the middle of December? I understand that they cannot use it prior to that date.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: MANITOBA GRAIN ACT-INSPECTION AND SALE OF GRAIN.
speechtext:
I doubt if there are enough buyers at Winnipeg to make the sample market a success, even if it were carried on all the year round. It is only an experiment, and my hon. friend is aware that there are great objections urged against the experiment by the railway companies on the ground that it is liable to tie up traffic. My view is that it is not advisable, in urging any changes, or what we think are improvements in connection with the grain trade, to create a position that might be blamed upon this advanced legislation, as we call it. We think it is better to go cautiously in this experiment, and not risk what the railway companies, who are good authorities on the subject, contend would be a serious disturbance of trade conditions, until we see how the matter is likely to work out. Therefore, it is provided that the provision as to an order point shall only prevail from the middle of December to the first of September. I move to insert the following as clause 7a of the Bill:
7a. The following section is inserted immediately after section 108 :
108a. Every elevator operator who allows the grain in a car which has been ordered east of Winnipeg or St. Boniface, from which he has signed a bill of lading and from which a sample of grain has been drawn for inspection as provided in subsection 3 of section 123 of this Act, to be returned, without the permission of the grain inspector, to the elevator from which it was loaded shall, for each offence be liable to a penalty not exceeding $50.

maintopic: MANITOBA GRAIN ACT-INSPECTION AND SALE OF GRAIN.

mg, he can do so with the permission of the inspector. Does the minister think that it is in the interest of the grain producers of the west to allow that?

longs.'-No. 1 hard, No. 1 spring, or whatever it may be.
